abstracts.value: Data-driven machine learning algorithms represent an alternative to numerical or analytical modeling of vibrating objects for the purpose of extracting their material or geometric properties. Their performance is conditioned by the quality of the training dataset, which should contain all possible production configurations of the object and measurement conditions. In this work, we propose a data-augmentation method based on manipulations of the vibration properties rather than numerical signal post-processing. Instead of modifying the sample’s material or geometry, we connect an additional sensor and actuator to the sample and use low-latency electronics to control the feedback signal. This delivers an electromechanical system with tunable oscillation properties. This signal diversification method is demonstrated on the classification of correct and incorrect adhesion of two aluminum plates. The labeling accuracy of 67% on nine unknown test objects, when trained on a single unchangeable training object, increases to 83% when the variety of the training vibration signals is augmented by varying the parameters of the electrovibratory feedback. This provides advantages for industrial quality control, where a large number of reference training samples are not available.

titles.title: Data augmentation by an electro-vibratory feedback improves signal interpretation by neural networks

abstracts.value: This dissertation presents a search for low-energy neutrinos in temporal coincidence with gravitational wave events reported by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration during the fourth observing run (O4), using 499.0 days of data collected during the liquid scintillator phase of the SNO+ experiment. The search uses inverse beta decay (IBD), which is primarily sensitive to electron antineutrinos, and neutrino-proton elastic scattering, a complementary neutral current channel providing sensitivity to all neutrino flavors. Candidate events were identified using optimized reconstruction and event-selection criteria developed with Monte Carlo simulations and validated with background-only data. The IBD background rate was measured directly from data, naturally incorporating reactor antineutrinos, geoneutrinos, radioactive backgrounds, cosmogenic backgrounds, and accidental coincidences present during detector operation. A model-independent framework was developed using flat spectrum neutrino Monte Carlo samples, allowing the detector response to be evaluated as a function of neutrino energy and applied to different theoretical emission models. As part of this work, improvements were made to the SNO+ Monte Carlo simulation, including modifications to the IBD generator to produce a true flat neutrino spectrum and corrections to the implementation of the neutrino-proton elastic scattering cross section. Detector characterization studies, including measurements of the deployed scintillator light yield and investigations of detector timing and electronics performance, were also performed to validate the detector response used throughout the analysis. The final gravitational wave-coincident dataset contained 143 candidates overlapping stable SNO+ data-taking periods. After excluding candidates classified as terrestrial or unknown by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration, the final astrophysical sample used for compact binary merger fluence limits contained 126 gravitational wave candidates. No statistically significant neutrino excess was observed in either the IBD or neutrino-proton elastic scattering channels. The IBD search observed no coincident candidates in the final astrophysical gravitational wave sample, consistent with an expected background of 1.25 ± 0.09 events. The corresponding Feldman-Cousins 90% confidence level upper limit is N90stack = 1.47 signal events. Stacked average (per gravitational wave) upper limits on the electron antineutrino fluence were derived for both monoenergetic neutrino emission and model-dependent spectra, including thermal neutrino and core-collapse supernova-inspired models used as detector sensitivity benchmarks. The neutrino-proton elastic scattering search represents the first application of this all-flavor channel to a gravitational wave-coincident neutrino search. Using an optimized ±50 s coincidence window, 108424 candidate events were observed, consistent with the expected background of 108345 ± 786 events estimated from local sidebands. The observed 0.24σ fluctuation is consistent with the background-only hypothesis. For the final astrophysical gravitational wave sample, the Feldman-Cousins method gives a 90% confidence level upper limit of N90stack = 1479.6 signal events. These results are used to derive the first all-flavor neutrino-proton elastic scattering fluence limits associated with compact binary merger candidates. The resulting SNO+ IBD fluence limits improve upon previous liquid scintillator gravitational wave-neutrino searches by approximately an order of magnitude in the few-MeV energy region, primarily due to the larger fiducial target mass, increased gravitational wave sample size, and low background rate achieved in SNO+. The neutrino-proton elastic scattering results establish the first all-flavor MeV neutrino search through this interaction channel in coincidence with gravitational wave events. Together, these analyses extend previous multi-messenger searches performed by Borexino, KamLAND, and Super-Kamiokande and demonstrate the capability of SNO+ to search for weak neutrino signals associated with astrophysical transients.

titles.title: The Search for Mev-scale Neutrinos in Temporal Coincidence With o4 Gravitational Wave Events Using the Sno+ Experiment

abstracts.value: Realistic simulation of quantum key distribution (QKD) networks requires a combination of precise models of quantum channels and network functions. Unfortunately, existing QKD network simulators lack either rigorous quantum physics modeling or network key-management and routing protocols, which limit their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose a QKD network simulator with hyperparameter tuning (QKDSim-HT), a NetSquid-based simulator specialized for polarization-based discrete-variable QKD networks. Specifically, QKDSim-HT models properties in quantum physics (photon loss, polarization-dependent depolarization, detector inefficiencies, dark counts, and dead times) as well as advanced functionalities in networking algorithms (multi-hop key relay and adaptive routing). Extensive simulations over diverse topologies reveal that the networking performance varied with respect to the fundamental properties of quantum physics, such as depolarization, fiber length, and channel attenuation. As a representative use case of QKDSim-HT, simulation results from QKDSim-HT over simple examples clearly manifest that a design of QKD networks highly affects performance of the networks. Accordingly, QKDSim-HT can serve as a practical platform for performance evaluation and optimization of quantum secured network.

titles.title: Quantum Key Distribution Network Simulator With Hyperparameter Tuning for Realistic Performance Analysis

abstracts.value: We present a unified theoretical framework for analyzing both electrostatic two-stream and electromagnetic Weibel instabilities in counterstreaming electron-positron pair plasmas. Through systematic derivation of dispersion relations in non-relativistic and relativistic regimes, we demonstrate how the symmetric mass ratio fundamentally alters instability characteristics compared to electron-ion systems. The two-stream instability, driven by longitudinal electrostatic perturbations parallel to beam motion, exhibits enhanced growth rates in pair plasmas due to equal contributions from both species, with relativistic suppression scaling as γ0−3 for both electrons and positrons. The Weibel instability, arising from transverse electromagnetic modes perpendicular to streaming directions, lacks the heavy-ion stabilization present in electron-ion plasmas, producing broader unstable spectral ranges and modified saturation levels. We derive explicit conditions determining the relative dominance of each mechanism across parameter space defined by drift velocity, wavenumber orientation, and relativistic Lorentz factor. Our analysis shows that longitudinal two-stream modes dominate at small perpendicular wavenumbers and moderate drift velocities, while transverse Weibel modes become prevalent at high perpendicular wavenumbers and large velocity spreads or temperature anisotropies. These findings have direct implications for understanding magnetic field generation, particle acceleration, and energy dissipation in astrophysical pair plasmas including pulsar wind nebulae, gamma-ray burst internal shocks, and active galactic nuclei jets where counterstreaming pair populations naturally arise.

titles.title: Suppression of two-stream and Weibel instabilities in ultra-relativistic electron–positron plasma

abstracts.value: Realistic quantum devices are open systems, and their behaviour depends not only on the subsystem of interest but also on how the environment is modelled and how the relevant observables are extracted. This thesis studies that problem in three settings. First, we study cavity-assisted qubit readout beyond the dispersive regime. We show that once coherent excitation exchange and dissipation become relevant, a microscopic treatment is needed to describe the readout quantitatively, and the optimal readout is set by a trade-off between signal accumulation and the distinguishability of the readout states. Second, we compare fermionic and spin baths in non-interacting transport models and show that spin baths reproduce fermionic reduced dynamics only in the large-bath weak-coupling limit, while clear deviations appear for smaller baths and near half-filling. Third, we study charge transport in molecular junctions using Automated Compression of Environments (ACE). There, the main difficulty is not the time evolution itself, but the extraction of the transport current, since this observable depends on system-environment correlations and is therefore not contained in the reduced system density matrix alone. We show that a probe-mode construction provides a viable route to reformulate the current as a system observable. This thesis advances our understanding of what is required for accurate modelling of open quantum dynamics across a range of solid-state settings, from cavity-assisted qubit readout to charge transport in molecular junctions.

titles.title: Developing and validating models of open quantum systems in solid-state nanostructures

abstracts.value: Using superconducting rectifiers to energize high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets is a promising approach to accelerate the uptake of HTS magnet technology. In this work, we start to address two limitations of the HTS superconducting rectifier concepts published to date; their low magnet charging voltages, and the variable properties of their HTS-based switches. Our approach is to test a centre-tapped full-wave transformer–rectifier utilizing HTS secondary windings and switch-arrays of Si <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small>s mounted on a printed-circuit board (PCB). This approach has the advantage of greatly facilitating reproducible and reliable manufacture. The rectifier demonstrated magnet charging voltages exceeding a cycle-averaged 80 mV at 100 A and with typically more than 30% of the power supplied to the primary coils delivered to the magnet. We found it to be resilient to our preliminary thermal-cycling testing, with no degradation in performance observed over eight liquid-nitrogen to ambient (77–295 K) thermal cycles. We compare the impact of voltage- and current-controlled modes for the rectifier’s power supply. Our conclusion is that superconducting rectifiers using <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small> switch arrays placed on PCBs is a very promising approach for low-current HTS magnet power supplies.

titles.title: Using Printed Circuit Boards and MOSFET Switch Arrays Toward the Reliable Manufacture of Superconducting Rectifiers

abstracts.value: Compact high turns ratio superconducting transformers are used to transfer power between low-current copper/ semiconductor-based circuits and high-current superconductor-based circuits. This type of transformer is a key component in devices, such as superconducting transformer rectifiers and superconducting current source inverters. Typically the copper winding and the superconducting winding are arranged with a turn ratio above 100:1, respectively, and are situated entirely within a cryogenic environment. The ohmic losses associated with the high count copper winding is problematic for most cryogenic applications and demands attention even when low currents on the order of 1–10 A are used. To address this problem, a transformer has been made using rare-earth barium copper oxide (REBCO) high-temperature superconductor (HTS) coated conductor for both the primary and secondary windings. The coupling coefficient and power consumption of this transformer were measured and compared to an equivalent transformer consisting of a copper primary winding and HTS secondary winding. The HTS primary was found to provide a significant reduction in transformer power consumption and a slight improvement to transformer coupling at frequencies below <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. An increased transformer core loss and winding AC loss began to negate these efficiency improvements above <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. In addition, cowinding the primary and secondary windings provided a higher coupling coefficient and lower power consumption for all winding combinations and frequencies tested. Finally, a short discussion on the implications of these findings respect to superconducting transformer rectifiers contextualizes the findings.

titles.title: Compact High Turns Ratio Superconducting Transformer: Comparison Between Cu and REBCO Winding Materials

abstracts.value: This article investigates the mechanical characteristics and critical current performance of aluminum-stabilized stacked REBCO tape cable (ASTC) for the circular electron-positron collider detector magnet. In-plane bending, torsion, and uniaxial tension tests are carried out, combined by finite element analysis. The correlation between critical current and strain under different loading conditions is systematically analyzed, and key mechanical thresholds are determined. Results show that the minimum allowable in-plane bending diameter is 1200 mm. The critical twist pitch is 327 mm. The critical current degrades to 95% of the initial value when the tensile strain in the REBCO tape reaches 0.37%. This study provides essential experimental data and theoretical support for the structural design and engineering application of ASTC in high-field superconducting magnets.

titles.title: Mechanical Characteristics of Aluminium-Stabilized Stacked REBCO Tape Cable for the CEPC Detector Magnet

abstracts.value: The development of large-scale superconducting quantum computers critically depends on the accurate readout of qubit states. To enable this, cryogenic parametric amplifiers have been proposed and developed, and have since found widespread use in small-signal detection applications. Among various amplifier architectures, Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) are widely adopted due to their broad bandwidth, high saturation power, and compatibility with superconducting qubits. In this work, we present a design workflow of JTWPAs based on a cosimulation approach combining electromagnetic (EM) and circuit-level simulation. We apply this method to a uniform JTWPA, comparing our simulation results with experimental data. To mitigate the challenge of constructing lumped-element circuit models usually used in the conventional simulation method, we directly perform full EM analysis of the device to accurately determine its linear response. The extracted S-parameters are then fed into a nonlinear harmonic balance simulator with Josephson junctions modeled as circuit elements. By doing so, the linear and gain properties of the JTWPA are extracted. Different factors that impact device performance including gain compression, phase matching, and fabrication imperfections are further investigated and modeled. A good agreement between simulation and measurements is identified, establishing the effectiveness of our approach in designing quantum parametric amplifiers.

titles.title: Designing Josephson Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifiers: EM-Circuit Cosimulation and Experimental Validation

abstracts.value: The q-plate is a spatially inhomogeneous SU(2) birefringent optical element that has garnered significant interest due to its ability to mediate the spin-orbit interaction of light and facilitate the generation of structured light with singularities. The q-plate features a spatially varying fast axis orientation defined by three parameters: the topological charge q, retardance delta, and the offset angle $alpha_0$. While the parameter alpha_0 can be changed many times by rotation, any change in the charge and/or retardance entails the fabrication of a new plate. This limitation can be overcome through the concept of an effective waveplate, where multiple waveplates, homogeneous or inhomogeneous, are aligned coaxially so that, under specific constraints, the composite system emulates the behavior of a single effective waveplate. This work presents a comprehensive mathematical formalism for realizing an effective waveplate through a cascaded configuration of three q-plates, each chosen as either a quarter-wave q-plate, a half-wave q-plate, or a combination thereof. Some configurations offer tunability of the retardance over the full range from 0 to $2pi$, even though q-plates with fixed retardances of $pi/2$ and pi are used in sequence to form an effective q-plate. This feature enables holonomic polarization walk on the higher-order Poincare sphere. Such a capability holds significant potential for applications involving structured light associated with the higher-order Poincare sphere, particularly in controlled polarization transformations and polarization-topology engineering.

titles.title: Mathematics of effective q-plate in polarization optics

abstracts.value: A Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) based Physical Layer Security (PLS) scheme (QKD-PLS) for optical fiber links is proposed and evaluated. In detail, a novel amplitude and phase scrambling technique for exploiting and seamlessly integrating high key rate QKD for the encryption of the modulation parameters of conventional complex modulation schemes like M-ary Quadrature Amplitude Modulation (M-QAM) and Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) is described. Scrambling is applied to both preamble (pilot signals) and payload segments of the transmission frame, to prevent the eavesdroppers from performing vital receiver functionalities such as frame synchronization and channel estimation. Additionally, a practical Key Management System (KMS) taking care of all key synchronization processes is developed and introduced. Moreover, another advantage of QKD exploitation to the proposed solution comes from the application of high entropy kbps-rate QKD keys feeding pseudo-random number generators, to modify the broadband modulation symbols in one-time pad, therefore significantly improving data protection. Experimental evaluation via a transmission scenario in fiber links is also presented, depicting the efficacy of the QKD-PLS.

titles.title: Quantum Key Distribution Based Physical Layer Security Applied in Complex Modulation Formats for Optical Fiber Links

abstracts.value: Black holes pose a lot of unsolved problems surrounding their fundamental properties. One of those puzzles is the black hole entropy problem. It has been known for a long time that black holes behave as thermodynamic systems and possess an entropy, but the question remains which microstates are responsible for this entropy. A theory of quantum gravity is needed to tackle this problem, currently the most viable example of which is string theory. The work of Strominger and Vafa, where they studied a class of asymptotically flat black holes, proves that string theory is indeed rich enough to account for the microstates responsible for the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy. Recently, the focus has shifted to asymptotically AdS black holes after the discovery of the AdS/CFT correspondence.Holographic dualities, the first example of which was discovered by Maldacena, have proven to be highly successful in providing a microstate counting for the entropy of black holes. The black hole is constructed on the gravity side of the correspondence, and the dual field theory counts its states. In this thesis we study black holes in AdS5 and their dual 4d N=1 SCFTs. The general procedure can be summarized as follows. On the field theory side, supersymmetric states are counted using the superconformal index. From the index we can obtain the entropy via a Legendre transform. By requiring that the entropy is real, we obtain a prediction for the existence of a dual black hole with that same entropy. In the dual supergravity theory we look for such solutions and compute the Euclidean on-shell action to match to the index, and the horizon area to match to the CFT entropy.This procedure was successfully applied to the minimal sector of any AdS5/CFT4 duality by Cabo-Bizet, Cassani, Martelli and Murthy, to leading order in the large N expansion. Here we aim to move beyond these results by adding flavour symmetries to the problem and by going beyond leading order at large N. On the field theory side of the duality, we study the index and entropy of flavoured SCFTs. We observe that for some theories, the simple procedure for taking the Legendre transform in the literature can no longer be applied. In all previously known examples, the index satisfies a cubic identity which leads to a simple way of deriving the entropy. We show that this identity no longer holds for certain theories but can be replaced by a sixth order identity, resulting in a different, more complicated expression for the entropy. These results suggest the existence of a new class of dual black hole solutions to match this entropy with their horizon area.We then proceed to finding these new solutions. This is a highly nontrivial problem because the dual supergravity theories contain hypermultiplet scalars. We specifically choose to work in the duality derived from M5-branes wrapping around a Riemann surface, between a family of non-Lagrangian class S SCFTs and a set of N=2 supergravities with two vector multiplets and one hypermultiplet, both parametrized by a rational number z. For z=±1, the cubic identity is satisfied and the entropy takes the familiar, simple form. Here we can easily identify the dual black holes through a relation to the five-dimensional STU model. For other values of z, we need the sixth order identity and we must include the hypermultiplet scalars in the black hole solution. To simplify the problem, we look for the near-horizon extremal geometry and restrict to two equal angular momenta. We start from the known solution for z=1 and perform an expansion around this point. We find an analytical solution to first order in the expansion. Since we only solve in the near-horizon region, we lose access to the on-shell action and chemical potentials but can still compute the charges and the entropy. The entropy through the area law matches precisely with the field theory prediction. We therefore prove that these partial solutions are the first step towards identifying the new class of black hole solutions with non-zero hypermultiplet scalars.In the final part of this thesis we move beyond the leading order at large N and add higher-derivative corrections. We focus on the universal case where only the R-symmetry is turned on. In this case, the higher-derivative action including four derivatives can be fully determined up to two constants, which can be related to the conformal anomalies of the dual field theory using the holographic map. We then set out to confirm the first subleading corrections to the index and entropy from the gravity side of the duality. We argue that the corrections to the black hole solution are not needed for the Euclidean on-shell action. It suffices to substitute the leading order solution in the corrected action. We perform this calculation carefully and obtain a precise match with the superconformal index. For the entropy, the corrections to the solution are needed. Here we opt to compute the entropy from the quantum statistical relation and the first law. Finally, we comment on higher-derivative corrections to flavoured theories.

titles.title: Holography and the Quantum Nature of Black Holes

abstracts.value:
One of the striking achievements of supersymmetric field theory was to
recast difficult perturbative statements in increasingly compact
structures governed by symmetry, analyticity, holomorphy, and geometry.
In four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetric Yang--Mills theory, the phrase
``one-loop exact'' records this development especially clearly.  This
survey reconstructs the quantum-field-theoretic statements compressed
into that phrase.  Early multiloop calculations and supergraph/background-field methods established an ultraviolet theorem about higher-loop
gauge-coupling counterterms.  Work on $\mathcal{N}=2$ quantization, dimensional
reduction, and invariant regulators then exposed the prescriptions needed
to realize that theorem in perturbation theory.  Anomaly and holomorphy
arguments reorganized the protected information in terms of distinguished
Wilsonian couplings, while Seiberg's 1988 formulation connected it to
non-perturbative physics.  In Seiberg--Witten theory the same slogan came
to describe the perturbative truncation of the Coulomb-branch
prepotential, whose exact form nevertheless contains instanton
corrections.  We distinguish holomorphic Wilsonian, canonically normalized,
1PI, and Coulomb-branch couplings and show explicitly why finite scheme
changes delimit all-orders beta-function statements.  The pre-Seiberg
origin of the non-renormalization theorem is well preserved in specialist
literature; priority revision is therefore not the main claim.  Rather,
the history is treated as a sequence of translations from ultraviolet
renormalization to holomorphic low-energy geometry.  Recovering the QFT
vocabulary of counterterms, regulators, Ward identities, prescriptions,
and effective actions identifies the physical content that the later,
more economical language encodes.

titles.title: The Changing Meaning of One-Loop Exactness in $\mathcal{N}=2$ Supersymmetric Yang--Mills Theory

Title: Geodesic motion in quadratic gravity spacetimes

Author: Bc. Matyáš Bílek

Institute: Institute of Theoretical Physics

Supervisor: doc. RNDr. Robert Švarc, Ph.D.

Abstract: This thesis investigates whether Quadratic Gravity admits an accelerating black hole solution
beyond the Einstein C-metric — one carrying a non-vanishing Bach tensor, and thus genuinely distinct from
the black holes of General Relativity. Our diagnostic is the relative motion of freely falling test particles: in
an invariant, frame-projected form the equation of geodesic deviation yields a tidal matrix, which we give
for various Petrov types, and into which the Bach tensor enters as an effective geometric source. Taking the
spherical Schwarzschild–Bach black hole as a template, where the geodesic-deviation conditions single
out the Schwarzschild solution, we carry the same strategy to the accelerating C-metric-like ansatz in the
conformal-to-Kundt form. For a purely radial metric function 𝐻 (𝑟) the field equations close and return
only the vacuum C-metric. Allowing 𝐻 to depend on the polar coordinate as well renders the ansatz of
algebraic Weyl type II; requiring it to remain Weyl type D forces it back to the vacuum C-metric, and
imposing instead only tidal indistinguishability from an Einstein spacetime reaches the same conclusion
on the C-metric background — off that background, we are not able to solve the system. The existence of
a genuinely non-Einstein accelerating black hole is left as an open problem.

Keywords: quadratic gravity, exact solutions, geodesic deviation, C-metric

Introduction
The study of the gravitational force has been with humanity for a long time. After the correction to

Newton’s theory that Einstein brought with his General Relativity, several contemporary physicists doubted
that it could be correct. Yet to this day the theory keeps a clean score: every experiment made agrees with
its theoretical predictions [1], and many further predictions have since been confirmed, the direct detection
of gravitational waves among the most striking [2]. It is, however, a real loss for theoretical physics
today that the predictions now being made can no longer be straightforwardly verified, the observable
effects being too small for the instruments of this era to measure — as is the case for the higher-derivative
extensions of General Relativity. These enlarge the space of predictions and solutions of General Relativity,
yet their effects are either too small, their coupling constants too loosely constrained, or their equations
too difficult to solve to reach a verdict. And just as some, at the dawn of General Relativity, declared it
incorrect, so to those who dismiss the higher-derivative theories we say: it is easy to judge; it is more
difficult to understand.

Among these higher-derivative theories the most natural first step is also the simplest: to add to the
Einstein–Hilbert action the terms quadratic in the curvature. This theory is called Quadratic Gravity,
and the addition of these terms makes the action renormalizable [3]. If we treat it as a quantum field
theory, the gravitational interaction becomes, at least formally, as well behaved as the other fundamental
interactions [4]. If we restrict ourselves to four dimensions, the action of Quadratic Gravity can be written
in a cleaner form: the Gauss–Bonnet combination is a pure surface term and its contribution drops out of
the field equations, so the entire freedom of the theory rests in two coupling constants, one multiplying the
square of the Weyl tensor and one the square of the scalar curvature. The theory is not without its troubles
— chief among them a massive ghost mode — but these are difficulties to be understood, not verdicts to be
pronounced.

Adding the quadratic terms does not discard General Relativity but enlarges it: every Einstein
spacetime still solves the field equations, so for example the Schwarzschild and C-metric geometries carry
over untouched. The genuinely new content of the theory lies in its non-Einstein solutions, for which
the Bach tensor no longer vanishes. Their static prototype is the Schwarzschild–Bach black hole [5], an
asymptotically Schwarzschild geometry carrying an extra invariant degree of freedom — a “Bach hair” —
with no counterpart in Einstein’s theory. This raises a natural question: by what invariant, in principle
observable, criterion can such a solution be told apart from an ordinary Einstein black hole? The answer
we pursue is the equation of geodesic deviation [6], which governs the relative acceleration of nearby
freely falling particles and is a purely geometric statement, independent of the field equations. Projected
onto an observer’s frame it defines a tidal matrix that splits into a Weyl part, common to both theories, and
a Bach part, present only in Quadratic Gravity. Turning the question around, one may instead demand that
these two contributions conspire so that a non-Einstein solution becomes tidally indistinguishable from its
Einstein counterpart — a condition that, applied to an accelerating black hole, is the guiding idea of the
final chapter.

The thesis is organized as follows. Chapter 1 collects the geometric and algebraic tools on which the
rest of the work builds: the description of spacetime curvature, the Newman–Penrose formalism, and the
algebraic classification of the curvature tensors in four and in higher dimensions.

Chapter 2 introduces the two gravitational theories we work with, General Relativity and Quadratic
Gravity. We present two exact solutions to General Relativity, namely the Schwarzschild black hole and
the C-metric, and the Schwarzschild–Bach black hole, the static prototype of a genuinely non-Einstein
solution to Quadratic Gravity.

Chapter 3 develops the central tool of the thesis, the equation of geodesic deviation in its projected,
frame-adapted form. We first present it in a theory-agnostic form, then in General Relativity, and finally in
Quadratic Gravity, where the Bach tensor enters the relative acceleration of nearby test particles.

Building on this, Chapter 4 turns to accelerating black holes in Quadratic Gravity, deriving their field
equations and analyzing their geodesic deviation, and asking whether requiring a non-Einstein solution to

7



be tidally indistinguishable from its Einstein counterpart can help single one out.
Finally, two appendices collect the technical material: Appendix A tabulates the tidal matrices for

each algebraic type, and Appendix B records the Newman–Penrose field equations used throughout.

Throughout this thesis we adopt the metric signature (−,+,+,+) and geometrized units in which
𝑐 = 𝐺 = 1, so that the gravitational coupling constant takes the value k = 16𝜋. Lowercase Latin indices

1 Theoretical background
This chapter presents the geometric framework of this work. Our approach relies on describing

spacetime as a differentiable manifold equipped with a Lorentzian metric in 𝐷 dimensions (typically we
fix 𝐷 = 4), allowing for the definition of curvature, geodesics, and their relative behavior.

Particular emphasis is placed on the equation of geodesic deviation, which provides a direct link
between the curvature of the manifold and the relative motion of neighboring geodesics. This equation
will serve as a probe to the geometrical structure of spacetimes, as we will see, we can go quite far without
resorting to a gravitational theory.

For a better understanding and easier interpretation, we introduce a null frame and an orthonormal
frame. In the first, we will decompose the curvature tensor, and in the latter, we will interpret the curvature
components.

effects [11, 20, 24]. For the congruence generated by k,

• 𝜅 measures its failure to be geodesic: the integral curves of k are null geodesics if and only if 𝜅 = 0;

• 𝜌 combines the expansion (the fractional rate of change of the cross-sectional area of a bundle of

and a vanishing 𝜌 a non-expanding one;

• 𝜎 is the complex shear, encoding the distortion of an initially circular bundle of rays into an ellipse;
𝜎 = 0 characterizes a shear-free congruence.

1.4 Algebraic classification of the curvature tensors
The curvature tensors introduced above contain the complete local geometric information of the

manifold, but their full component structure is often too complicated for direct analysis. A natural
simplification is obtained by studying their algebraic structure, that is, by classifying them according to
the existence of preferred directions, degeneracies, and canonical forms in suitably adapted frames. In this
work, we will decompose the Riemann tensor into the Weyl and Ricci tensors. Thus we will provide an
outlook of the algebraic classification of those two tensors here.

From a geometric point of view, the Weyl tensor describes the conformally invariant part of curvature

The key concept in this description is the algebraic type of the Weyl tensor, which is defined through
the existence of preferred null directions and the vanishing of chosen frame components [12, 13]. This
classification is independent of any particular gravitational theory and, up to some point, spacetime
dimension.

projections which generalize the usual Newman–Penrose Weyl scalars to arbitrary dimension. These

2 Gravitational theories
In the previous chapter, the geometric quantities entering the description of spacetime curvature were

introduced independently of any specific gravitational theory. This framework can describe a physical
reality, by relating the curvature dynamics to matter dynamics through field equations, Albert Einstein
achieved just that. In this chapter, we therefore summarize the field equations of General Relativity and
Quadratic Gravity, and then formulate the equation of geodesic deviation in a projected frame form suitable
for their comparison. In this way, one can clearly distinguish between the purely geometric structure of the
relative acceleration and its theory-dependent part.

2.1 General Relativity
General Relativity describes gravity as the curvature of a Lorentzian spacetime which is related to the

distribution of matter and energy. Within this framework, freely falling test particles move along timelike
geodesics, while the gravitational force is represented by the non-flatness of the underlining geometry.
The central relation between geometry and the matter sources is provided by Einstein’s field equations,
which connect the Ricci curvature to the energy-momentum tensor [7, 8].

2.1.3 Some solutions
Having set out the field equations of General Relativity, we now record the two exact vacuum solutions

that will serve as the reference geometries of this work: the static Schwarzschild black hole and its uniformly
accelerated generalization, the C-metric. Both are Einstein spacetimes with a vanishing Ricci tensor,
and both are algebraically special — of Petrov type D in the classification of the previous chapter. The
Schwarzschild solution is the arena in which the elementary features of a black hole are most transparent,
while the C-metric introduces the single new ingredient — acceleration — that lies at the heart of the
present thesis.

The C-metric
The single most important generalization for the present work is obtained by allowing the black hole

to accelerate. The resulting exact vacuum solution is the C-metric [26], so named by Ehlers and Kundt in
their 1962 classification [37], although the static form of the metric had already been written down by
Levi-Civita in 1918 and by Weyl in 1919 [38, 39] and was subsequently rediscovered many times. Its
physical meaning was clarified by Kinnersley and Walker [40] and by Bonnor [41]: taken together with its
analytic extension, the C-metric describes a pair of causally separated black holes that accelerate away
from one another under the action of cosmic strings or struts, represented by conical singularities along
the axis [42].

3 Projected geodesic deviation
The two solutions constructed in the previous chapter — the Schwarzschild and the Schwarzschild–

Bach black holes — are Einstein and non-Einstein representatives of the same static, spherically symmetric
ansatz, and they were seen to differ by a single invariant, the value of the Bach tensor. It remains to make
this difference physical: to exhibit a concrete, locally measurable effect that distinguishes an Einstein
geometry from a genuinely Quadratic Gravity one.

The natural instrument is the relative motion of nearby freely falling test particles, governed by the
equation of geodesic deviation [15]. As stressed already in the first chapter, this equation is a purely
geometric statement — it links the curvature to the observed tidal accelerations without reference to any
field equations — so that the same framework serves both theories, and their difference is read off from the
way the field equations fix the curvature. This chapter develops that framework in full, first for a general
spacetime, then in General Relativity, and finally in Quadratic Gravity, where it becomes the principal tool
for detecting and, ultimately, constraining the non-Einstein solutions of the theory.

Conclusion
In the presented work we studied the relative motion of freely falling test particles as a diagnostic tool

of the genuinely non-Einstein content of four-dimensional Quadratic Gravity, with particular emphasis on
static and uniformly accelerating black holes. After introducing the necessary geometric framework we
reviewed the exact solutions on which the rest of the work relies: the Schwarzschild and C-metric geometries
of General Relativity, which remain solutions of Quadratic Gravity, and the static Schwarzschild–Bach
black hole, the prototype of a genuinely non-Einstein spacetime carrying a non-vanishing Bach tensor. We
then turned to the main original problem of the thesis: whether Quadratic Gravity admits a spacetime
with a uniformly accelerating black hole beyond the General Relativity C-metric, and by what locally
measurable effect such a solution could be distinguished from its General-Relativistic template.

The instrument developed for this purpose is the projected equation of geodesic deviation. Written in
an invariant, frame-adapted form, it delivers a tidal matrix, which splits cleanly into a Weyl part, common
to General Relativity and Quadratic Gravity, and a Ricci part, which is further determined by the used
theory. In Quadratic Gravity for vacuum solutions, the Ricci part is carried entirely by the Bach tensor and
therefore exclusive to Quadratic Gravity. This decomposition turns an abstract field-equation statement
into an observable one. As a first application, the requirement that the static Schwarzschild–Bach black
hole be tidally indistinguishable from an Einstein spacetime was shown to force its Bach parameter to
vanish, returning exactly the Schwarzschild geometry and providing the methodological template for the
accelerating case.

The principal result concerns a spacetime with a accelerated black hole. Recasting the C-metric into the
conformal-to-Kundt form and promoting its three metric functions to a general functions, we set up the full
Quadratic Gravity field equations together with the Newman–Penrose curvature scalars and the null-frame
components of the Bach tensor, and attacked the resulting system along three independent routes, as the
full system proves to be to difficult to integrate: a purely radial metric function 𝐻, the requirement that the
ansatz remains algebraically of type D, and the weaker requirement of tidal indistinguishability from an
Einstein spacetime. The first two converge on the same conclusion — the only accelerating black hole
they admit is the vacuum C-metric, on which the Bach source drops out identically. The third was only
integrated assuming the metric functions Ω and 𝑃 to be the same as in the C-metric, then we showed that
𝐻 also has to be of the form as in the C-metric. For general form of the three metric functions, the system
was still too coupled to be integrated.

The convergence to the C-metric is not accidental. Throughout the ansatz investigation the acceleration
parameter was taken to be non-vanishing, 𝛼 ≠ 0, which forces the conformal factor Ω to depend on the
polar coordinate; fed into the field equations, it is precisely this angular dependence that constrains the
radial metric function and annihilates the Bach source. Had the acceleration been switched off, 𝛼 = 0,
the same system would relax and readmit the static Schwarzschild–Bach solution, which is a genuine
non-Einstein solution. Within the ansatz studied here, acceleration and Bach hair stand in direct tension,
and the field equations of the theory prove restrictive.

While the results obtained are largely negative, they map out rather precisely where any genuinely
non-Einstein accelerating black hole could still be hiding. Several natural continuations of this work
therefore suggest themselves.

Firstly, a numerical or asymptotic treatment of that system, aimed at deciding whether it admits a
solution off the C-metric background, is the most direct continuation of the present work.

Second, it would be natural to enlarge the setting while retaining as much analytic control as possible,
by adding a cosmological constant, electric charge, or a NUT parameter to the background and asking
whether the same collapse to the Einstein solution persists. In view of the known exact generalizations
of the Schwarzschild–Bach family, such extensions are within reach and would test how much of the
restrictiveness observed here is specific to the pure-vacuum, uncharged case.

Third, the diagnostic tool developed here is not tied to the accelerating black hole solution. Applying
it to other algebraically special backgrounds — Taub–NUT among them — should help identify which

49



geometric features are truly responsible for the collapse to the Einstein solution, and to what extent the
mechanism survives outside the static, axially symmetric case, for instance on a rotating background.

Finally, because the tidal matrix is by construction an observable object, its Bach part invites a more
phenomenological study: the effect of the leading higher-derivative correction on the motion of test bodies,
on effective potentials, and on the characteristic tidal signatures that might, in principle, differentiate a
Quadratic Gravity black hole from its Einstein counterpart.

To summarize, the thesis develops the projected equation of geodesic deviation into an invariant tidal
diagnostic for Quadratic Gravity, in which the Bach tensor appears as an effective geometric source, and
applies it to static and uniformly accelerating black holes. It treats an accelerating ansatz, which is a
generalization of the C-metric. For three distinctive extra assumptions, it tackles the Quadratic Gravity
field equations of the ansatz, we have shown that under the first two assumption —that the metric function
𝐻 depends solely on the radial-like coordinate, that the ansatz should remain type D— falls back to the
C-metric. The third assumption was tackled, only with a determined metric function Ω and 𝑃, leaving
the solution with their general form an open question, as well as a solution of the unrestricted Quadratic
equations for the ansatz.

i

This doctoral thesis was supported by the Polish National Science Centre (NCN) OPUS project No.
2019/33/B/ST2/00613. and the Polish National Science Centre NCN Grant SONATA project No.

2020/39/D/ST2/02054



ii

Abstract

Because QCD is strongly coupled at low energies, standard perturbative techniques are no longer applicable
at this energy scale. In this thesis, we use effective models that have hadronic degrees of freedom. The
guiding principle throughout is the implementation of the global symmetries of QCD and their anomalous,
explicit, and spontaneous breaking patterns, notably chiral symmetry and dilatation symmetry.
First, the theory of a free scalar field coupled to a time-independent classical source is studied as a simplified
model for dilaton production in a medium. We show that the time evolution in the theory is non-trivial,
contrary to historical expectations. The theory exhibits nonperturbative particle production similar to the
Schwinger mechanism, with interesting features such as non-exponential decay and the quantum Zeno effect.
Next, we introduce the extended Linear Sigma Model (eLSM) and apply it to (axial) tensor mesons, the
tensor glueball, and charmonium states mixing with the vector glueball.
We confirm the quark-antiquark assignment of the standard tensor meson nonet by fitting their decays to
data. Using chiral symmetry, we derive predictions for the masses and decays of axial tensor mesons which
can be tested by experiments. The axial tensor mesons are predicted to be very broad states.
The eLSM is used to calculate decay ratios of the tensor glueball. We then compare these to experimental
data on known candidates for the tensor glueball. This comparison shows that the f2(1950) is the most
likely tensor glueball candidate in this framework. A rough estimate of the decay widths also indicates that
the tensor glueball could be a relatively broad state.
Finally, the decays of the charmonium states J/ψ and ψ(3686) into vector–pseudoscalar final states are inves-
tigated. These channels exhibit significant violations of the perturbative QCD “13% rule", most prominently
in the ρπ channel. We apply the eLSM, including electromagnetic effects and mixing with the vector glueball.
It is shown that these ingredients allow for a successful phenomenological description of the observed ratios
B(ψ(3686) → h)/B(J/ψ → h).



iii

Streszczenie

Fenomenologia kuł gluonowych w efektywnych modelach

hadronowych

Ponieważ QCD jest teorią silnie oddziałującą w reżimie niskich energii, standardowe techniki perturbacyjne
nie znajdują w tym zakresie zastosowania. W niniejszej rozprawie wykorzystujemy modele efektywne, w
których stopnie swobody mają charakter hadronowy. Zasadą przewodnią jest konsekwentna implementacja
globalnych symetrii QCD oraz wzorców ich łamania – anomalnego, jawnego i spontanicznego – ze szczegól-
nym uwzględnieniem symetrii chiralnej oraz dylatacyjnej.
W pierwszej części badana jest teoria swobodnego pola skalarnego oddziałującego z klasycznym, nieza-
leżnym od czasu źródłem, traktowana jako uproszczony model produkcji dylatonu w ośrodku. Pokazujemy,
że ewolucja czasowa w tej teorii jest nietrywialna, wbrew wcześniejszym oczekiwaniom. Teoria wykazuje
nieperturbacyjną produkcję cząstek, analogiczną do mechanizmu Schwingera, z interesującymi własności-
ami, takimi jak nieeksponencjalny rozpad oraz kwantowy efekt Zeno.
Następnie wprowadzamy extended Linear Sigma Model (eLSM) i stosujemy go do opisu mezonów (aksjalno-
)tensorowych, tensorowej kuli gluonowej oraz stanów charmonium mieszających się z wektorową kulą glu-
onową. Potwierdzamy standardowe przypisanie mezonów tensorowych do nonetu kwark–antykwark poprzez
dopasowanie ich szerokości rozpadów do danych doświadczalnych. Wykorzystując symetrię chiralną, wyprowadzamy
przewidywania dotyczące mas oraz rozpadów mezonów aksjalno-tensorowych, które mogą zostać zwery-
fikowane eksperymentalnie. Przewiduje się, że mezony aksjalno-tensorowe są stanami bardzo szerokimi.
Model eLSM jest następnie wykorzystywany do obliczenia stosunków rozpadów tensorowej kuli gluonowej.
Otrzymane wyniki porównujemy z danymi doświadczalnymi dotyczącymi znanych kandydatów na tensorową
kulę gluonową. Porównanie to wskazuje, że rezonans f2(1950) jest w tych ramach teoretycznych najbardziej
prawdopodobnym kandydatem na tensorową kulę gluonową. Przybliżone oszacowania szerokości rozpadu
sugerują ponadto, że tensorowa kula gluonowa może być stanem relatywnie szerokim.
W końcowej części analizowane są rozpady stanów charmonium J/ψ oraz ψ(3686) do stanów końcowych typu
wektor–pseudoskalar. Kanały te wykazują istotne naruszenia perturbacyjnej reguły QCD „13%”, szczególnie
wyraźne w kanale ρπ. Stosujemy model eLSM, uwzględniając efekty elektromagnetyczne oraz mieszanie z
wektorową kulą gluonową. Pokazujemy, że uwzględnienie tych składników umożliwia udany fenomenolog-
iczny opis obserwowanych stosunków B(ψ(3686) → h)/B(J/ψ → h).

Chapter 1

Introduction

In the 1970s, the Standard Model (SM) of particle physics was finalized, and it has since described our current
knowledge of the fundamental particles and their interactions. Although certain large-scale phenomena such
as dark matter, dark energy, and baryogenesis have not been explained by the SM, the SM has been extremely
successful in describing and predicting the results from particle physics experiments to the present day.
Notable predictions of the SM include anomalous magnetic dipole moments, and the existence of multiple
particles, including the W, Z and Higgs boson. The SM is a quantum field theory (QFT) based on local gauge
symmetries – internal symmetries of the fields that do not act on their spacetime coordinates – from which
the form of the fundamental interactions can be derived. The gauge symmetries of the SM are described by
the group

SU(3)× SU(2)×U(1). (1.0.1)

The SU(2)×U(1) describe the electroweak interactions, which at low energies are spontaneously broken by
the Higgs mechanism to just the electromagnetic U(1) gauge symmetry; electromagnetism and the weak
nuclear force are no longer unified. By this spontaneous symmetry breaking, mass terms for all the massive
fundamental particles are generated. In one of the models studied in this thesis the mechanism of sponta-
neous symmetry breaking is used in a similar manner to the Higgs mechanism and is a key ingredient of the
model, although with some differences, such as the kind of symmetry that is broken; in the Higgs mechanism
in the Standard Model a local symmetry is broken while for the effective model is it a global symmetry.
In this thesis we will be primarily interested in the strong nuclear force, which is described by the SU(3) part,
which together with the matter fields is called quantum chromodynamics (QCD). The standard method of
calculating quantities in QFT is via perturbation theory; the case in the full theory is regarded as a small
perturbation on a more simple, solvable theory, usually a free (noninteracting) theory. Quantities are then
calculated in a perturbative expansion in a small parameter, the coupling. In doing this it is important that
the coupling is small, which is not always the case for QCD. In particular, QCD has a property that is called
Asymptotic Freedom, which means that at high energies (small length scales) the coupling becomes weaker
and QCD approaches a free field theory at high energies, called the ultraviolet (UV) limit. Conversely,
at low energies and larger length scales around the size of hadrons such as the proton, QCD is strongly
coupled. In this regime, a perturbative expansion is not a reliable way to calculate observable quantities,
and effects which cannot be represented in a perturbative expansion, called nonperturbative effects, become
more significant.
While for weakly coupled systems perturbation theory is a very good universal method for computing ob-

CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 2

servables, for strongly coupled systems there is no approximation that is known to work for all kinds of
systems. Indeed there are numerous different methods for approximating QCD observables, each with their
own advantages and disadvantages. QCD also has a peculiar feature which is called confinement. Quarks and
gluons are the fundamental degrees of freedom (particles) of QCD, and they carry color charge. However,
asymptotic states, the ones we can see in detectors, are all color neutral. Experiments do not measure quarks
and gluons but composite particles in which the color charges cancel, called hadrons. This is called confine-
ment, and while it is not completely understood yet, a qualitative explanation is the gluon self-interaction
which forms a narrow flux tube between two color charged particles, when the particles are separated the
energy of the flux tube increases enough to form another quark-antiquark pair, making it so that if we try
to break up a hadron we just end up making more hadrons. Due to the self-interactions between gluons, a
special case of hadrons is predicted to appear in QCD, which are the glueballs, made up of only gluons. So
far they have only been predicted by theory, but are not conclusively found in any experiment. In this thesis
we will be especially interested in the behavior of glueballs and how we might detect them.
Given that the physical particles experiments detect are not the quarks and gluons but the hadrons, instead
of attempting to calculate observables from the behavior of quarks and gluons, one option is to directly
construct a theory of the hadronic degrees of freedom, which are able to be detected in experiments. This
is done in effective models, which will be the main focus of the thesis. The symmetries of QCD will be used
as a guiding principle in constructing the interactions in the model. For this purpose we will review the
basics of QCD in 1.1, with an emphasis on the (breaking of) symmetries. In 1.3 we will give a more detailed
overview of the topics of this thesis.

1.2 Bound states of QCD

Quarks and gluons are not the asymptotic physical states that we detect. While it is not rigorously derived
from QCD, we have understood that color charge and by extension color charged particles such as quarks
and gluons are confined. In other words, all detected particles are in a color singlet state. The composite
particles we can detect are hadrons, and are categorized into mesons and baryons. Mesons are defined by
having integer spin and thus being bosons, or equivalently by having vanishing baryon number B = 0, where
B = ±1/3 for (anti)quarks and B = 0 for gluons. Baryons are defined by being fermions or equivalently by
B = 1 baryon number.
Mesons can be further split up into conventional and unconventional mesons. Conventional mesons are made



CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 7

up of a quark and antiquark pair, while unconventional mesons are made of every other possibility, examples
are tetraquarks, glueballs (made of only gluons), and molecular states (made up by two spatially distinct
quark-antiquark pairs). While unconventional mesons have many more possibilities, the vast majority of
mesons listed in the PDG are interpreted as a quark-antiquark state. Mesons are classified by a few quantum
numbers. These are their spatial angular momentum L, their spin S, their total angular momentum J =

L+ S. From these the parity P and charge conjugation C eigenvales can be calculated as

P = (−1)L+1, C = (−1)L+S . (1.2.1)

Mesons are then labeled by JPC . For example, the previously mentioned pseudo-Goldstone bosons have
JPC = 0−+ and are pseudoscalars. Scalar mesons have JPC = 0++, and vector mesons have JPC =

1−−. In conventional mesons with nonrelativistic quarks, the spin of the quark-antiquark pair necessarily
sums up to either 1 or 0. When S = 0, it follows that J = L, P = −C and the only possibilities are

1.3 Outline of the thesis

In this thesis we will study effective models for QCD at the level of hadrons. We phenomenologically describe
and predict the behavior of certain hadron. A particular focus is given to glueballs and unconventional
hadrons. The thesis is based on the publications [13] (Chapter 2), [14] (Chapter 4), [15, 16, 17] (Chapter 5),
[18] (Chapter 6)
In chapter 2 we examine the theory of a free scalar field interacting with a time independent classical source,



CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION 8

as a model for the phenomenology of scalar glueballs in a post-collision medium. Historically it was believed
that on a time independent source there is no scattering and so the dynamics are trivial. We compute
scattering amplitudes exactly and show that this is not the case, but that the absence of scattering was a
result of the idea that one can switch off the interaction adiabatically. In fact this assumption does not hold
in this case, and particle production from the vacuum, conceptually similar to the Schwinger mechanism,
gives rise to scattering.
In chapters 3 we go over the construction of the extended Linear Sigma Model (eLSM), which is an effective
hadronic model based on the symmetries of QCD and their anomalous, explicit and spontaneous breaking
patterns. In its basic form it contains the dilaton (scalar glueball), pseudoscalars, scalars, vectors, and axial
vectors mesons. It can be readily extended to include more mesons such as higher spin mesons or different
glueballs. This is done in the following chapters. In chapter 4 we include the tensor and axial tensor mesons.
Experimentally, the ground-state tensor mesons are well known, but for the axial tensors the data on most
decay modes and masses are still missing. Due to the fact they are chiral partners, both of their interactions
can be described in a unified framework in the eLSM. From the eLSM we describe the decays of the tensor
mesons and predict some decay channels, and use this to predict the masses and decays of the axial tensor
mesons.
In chapter 5, we extend the eLSM to the tensor glueball. No glueball has yet been experimentally identified,
but the tensor is the second lightest glueball (after the scalar) according to lattice QCD calculations at
around 2 GeV, and therefore likely to be one of the easiest to find. There are a number of potential
candidate resonance which could be the tensor glueball, and we compare their known data to predictions we
make with the eLSM. From this, we conclude the f2(1950) is the most likely tensor glueball candidate.
In chapter 6 we study the decays of the J/ψ and ψ(2S) charmonium states in the eLSM. From perturbative
calculations in QCD it follows that these states should obey the so-called 13% rule, but for some decay
channels this rule is severely violated. The first discovered and biggest offender is the ρπ channel, and most
vector-pseudoscalar channels do not follow the 13% rule. We use the eLSM along with electromagnetic decay
channels, and allow the vector glueball to mix with the ψ(2S). Electromagnetic interactions turn out to be
crucial in order to agree with data, and the inclusion of the vector glueball improves the description as well.
With both these ingredients we reach a successful phenomenological description of the breaking of the 13%

rule of the V P decays of J/ψ and ψ(2S).

The scalar glueball with a time

2.1 Introduction

In the previous chapter we have seen that the gluons have a nonzero vacuum expectation value due to the
trace anomaly. In the presence of a medium, such as in matter or heavy-ion collisions, this expectation
value will pick up a spacetime dependence. This can then be modeled as a classical source of these particles,
which can form a scalar glueball. For example, particle production of a scalar field ϕ can manifest from a
self-interaction as follows

ϕ4(x) → ⟨ϕ⟩4x + 4 ⟨ϕ⟩3x ϕ(x) + ... (2.1.1)

One of these terms describes a ϕ field being created or annihilated by a source ⟨ϕ⟩3x. This is the model we
will study in depth in this chapter. This theory, which describes an uncharged free scalar particle coupled
to an external classical source, has received much attention during the early stages of the development of
quantum field theory. This is very natural given it is one of the simpler QFTs one can write down, and it
has become a textbook example illustrating concepts in quantum field theory [19, 20, 21, 22].
The common belief that was held in the past is that if the classical source is static in time, the theory has no
scattering and the time evolution is trivial. We will take a close look at the arguments used for this claim and
give reasoning as to why it can be disputed. Namely, in this chapter we calculate the exact time evolution
of quantum states, in particular states with definite particle number (and momentum). It turns out that in
the specific case of a time-independent source, the scattering is not trivial, but caused by particle production
from the (particle) vacuum. This vacuum decays in a similar fashion as in the Schwinger mechanism. In
fact, this vacuum decay, together with absorption of incoming particles by the source, is the key element to
solve all the dynamics of the system, whatever the initial state.
Vacuum decay is often described in terms of a metastable or false vacuum, which is a state at a local min-
imum of the Hamiltonian1, which then decays due to tunneling. In this context, vacuum decay of scalar
fields has been studied extensively for example by using thin wall approximations [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29],
which in certain situations is analogous to quantum mechanical tunneling [30]. A possible experimental test

of false vacuum decay is proposed in [31, 32]. One important application is the study of the electroweak
vacuum of the Higgs potential [33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38]. Quantum corrections to the Higgs self-interaction
can turn the minimum, which classically is a global one, to just a local minimum. Whether or not this
happens and the electroweak vacuum is a false vacuum depends on the parameters, in particular, the Higgs
mass and the top quark mass. According to current measurements and calculations it is indeed metastable
[34, 35, 36] with a lifetime longer than the age of the universe. It is however close enough to stability that
further studies and precise measurements are required. The presence of gravity also has interesting effects
on vacuum stability and vice versa, see e.g. [24, 39, 40, 41]. Recently it has been shown that also in the
non-interacting case nontrivial vacua can be necessary to properly renormalize the expectation values of
observables in flat [42, 43], as well as curved spacetimes and cosmologies [44, 45]. Non-trivial vacuum effects
have also been shown to be a relevant source of particles in heavy-ion collisions [42, 46].
Aside from serving as an effective description for dilaton production in the presence of a medium such as
a quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ion collisions, the perturbation of a ground state by a (temporary) classical
external field can be a convenient way to approximate various physical phenomena. Besides the many scalar
fields in hadron physics, beyond the Standard Model physics often have new scalar particles as well, such as
the inflaton in cosmology.

This vacuum decay process for scalar fields is conceptually analogous to the Schwinger mechanism [47,
48, 49, 30], in which particle-antiparticle pairs are created nonperturbatively from the vacuum in the pres-
ence of a strong static electric field. Past the conceptual similarity, the methods and results in this chapter
are different. While the Schwinger mechanism is a nonperturbative effect, is it still based on further approx-
imations, beyond the classical source, while we will have a class of exact solutions instead. In the Schwinger
mechanism there is particle-antiparticle pair production, in contrast to our case, in which a single particle
production, and by extension any number of particles, is possible. Whereas in the Schwinger mechanism the
vacuum decay is exponential, in this chapter we will see the The vacuum decay does not follow an exponen-
tial. In fact, the vacuum survival probability eventually saturates at large times, so that the final particle
number expectation is constant. In particular, the survival probability is quadratic at short times, thus
allowing for the quantum Zeno effect if repeated measurements are performed. The quantum Zeno effect is
realized when the time evolution of a system can frozen by repeated measurements at short time intervals
and occurs when the decay law at short times is slower than an exponential, see e.g. [50, 51, 52, 53, 54]. It
is an important effect in cavity QED [55, 56] and potentially even in large systems when gravity is involved
[57]. In the case of the anti Zeno effect [54, 58, 59] the decay is accelerated by repeated measurements with
longer time intervals. They are both generic results of quantum mechanics and quantum field theory, but in
most cases - for example the decay of muons - an exponential decay is an extremely good approximation. In
many systems an exponential is such a good approximation that it is experimentally indistinguishable from
the full decay law. In the vacuum decay studied in this chapter this is not the case; there is no time scale
where an exponential decay is a good approximation for the full decay formula.
We start off with describing the system in subsection 2.2. In subsection 2.3 we derive exact scattering am-
plitudes and probabilities of the vacuum decaying to n particles. In subsection 2.4 we focus on the vacuum
decay, and look at the small time and large time behaviors. Some specific forms of the external sources are
taken as examples and we calculate the vacuum decay probability distribution for these, and find the behavior
for large volume. In subsection 2.5 We compare the findings to previous work and discuss phenomenological
applications. Finally, we conclude in subsection 2.6.

2.3.1 General expressions

Given a generic initial state of the system |ψi⟩ measured or prepared at time ti = 0, the probability amplitude
and probability to measure the state |ψf ⟩ at a later time t > 0 are given by the time-evolution operator of
the theory U(t, 0) by

ai→f (t) = ⟨ψf |U(t, 0)|ψi⟩ , Pi→f (t) = |ai→f (t)|2 . (2.3.1)

The operator U(t, 0) is also referred to as the ‘propagator’ [19, 60], but this should not be confused with the
Feynman propagator or similar quantities. These other quantities will not be as relevant for this chapter
and so we will use the names evolution-time operator or propagator interchangeably in this chapter.
The probability amplitude simplifies significantly when the Hamiltonian is time independent. For a time
independent source, the Hamiltonian is also time independent. When the source depends on time then so
will the Hamiltonian, and solving (2.3.1) becomes a nontrivial task. Before focusing on the case for the static
source, we will solve the dynamics for an arbitrary source, and simplify to a static source later on. One
way to tackle this problem is to fully calculate the Dyson series. However, since we have the full solutions
to the equation of motion at all time (2.2.9), it is possible to avoid solving for the propagator U(t, 0), by
taking a small detour into some unphysical states. Any uncharged scalar field can be decomposed in terms
of time-dependent ladder operators in the form (2.2.9). This allows us to use all the free-field concepts of

the particle number eigenstates built with the free field are the particle number eigenstates of the interacting
scalar field at t = 0. In the Heisenberg picture the physical states do not evolve in time, therefore the states
at time t0 = 0 are the physical states at all times.

2.5 Comparison to literature

The quantum field theory of a real scalar field coupled to a classical external source is one of the simplest
interacting QFTs one can write down. Unsurprisingly, It has been studied in the past and it has been
mentioned or discussed in textbooks as an example of calculations in QFT, see e.g. [19, 20, 21, 22]. For a
time dependent source ρ(t,x) which is Fourier transformable in spacetime, it is commonly accepted that the
dynamics can be nontrivial. The case of a time independent source is then treated as a limit of the time
dependent case. Specifically, the time independent classical source is multiplied by an adiabatic function of
time that switches off the interaction in the distant past and future. In the limit where the interaction persists
for infinite amount of time, the scattering matrix is found to be essentially the identity matrix. This is usually
assumed to imply an equivalence between the interacting system (without the adiabatic function) and a free
quantum field theory and so there is no scattering. Since some of the intuitive statements commonly used are
incomplete, and it is easy to miss some fundamental conceptual steps looking just at the scattering matrix,
we will go into a more detailed discussion.

nontrivial scattering amplitudes, contradict the results found in the literature. We will refer in particular
to the analysis in the seminal lectures on QFT by Coleman [20], since the treatment is rather extensive
and it inspired some of the other books on QFT, such as [22], especially on the triviality of scattering on a
time independent source. The starting point is the exact solution for the case of a time dependent source,
