and degrees of freedom of a stack of n coincident M5-branes has been a longstanding problem
[86].

Despite the great interest the BFSS matrix model has received in the past three decades, many
pieces of the puzzle are still missing. Its structure makes computations of scattering amplitudes
technically involved and the limit in which it is defined is not directly related to the standard
strong coupling limit relating type IIA string theory to M-theory. Nevertheless, the fact that in
this framework both dynamical and gravitational effects appear to be of quantum nature is a
very attractive feature for a candidate quantum gravity theory. BFSS has also been related to
holography since the strongly-coupled large-N regime of the D0-brane quantum mechanics is
conjectured to be dual to the near-horizon black D0-brane geometry in type IIA supergravity
and has been used in related numerical tests [87]. For a more recent study on the relation
between BFSS and holography see e.g. [88].

Matrix models need not be considered only in the context of M-theory. Notable examples are the
Ishibashi-Kawai-Kitazawa-Tsuchiya (IKKT) model for type IIB [89, 90], the Itoyama–Tsuchiya
model for type I [91] and matrix string theory for type IIA [92–94].

The above analysis indicates the attractive features of probing the microscopic structure of
M-theory, but can also serve as a warning that it is a formidable task, with many aspects still

Chapter 2

Swampland Program and Emergence

This chapter aims to provide a focused review of the swampland program, with particular
emphasis on its aspects relevant for the present thesis. The interested reader can obtain a
broader overview, for example through the following reviews and notes [33, 95–99].

2.1 Overview

At this point, we have reviewed some fundamental aspects of string theory and M-theory. In
doing so, we have already encountered the supergravity actions used as low-energy descriptions
of string theory. What we have not yet done is discuss to what extent these are compatible
with general expectations of effective field theories. On a fundamental level, properties such as
unitarity seem reasonable both from a string theory and an effective field theory perspective,
while modular invariance, for instance, has no obvious analog within ordinary effective field
theory. On the string theory side, a principle or mechanism capable of distinguishing among
the vast number of background solutions for string theory, corresponding to different choices
of background fields and fluxes, is needed. The swampland program aims to address the
complementary issue of whether quantum gravity considerations render seemingly consistent
effective field theories incompatible with an ultraviolet completion.

The central idea of the swampland program [100] is that only a subset of the effective field
theories that appear consistent, for example, by satisfying requirements such as the absence of
anomalies and unitarity, can admit an ultraviolet completion within a theory of quantum gravity.
This subset is called the (quantum gravity) landscape, while the rest form the swampland. A
schematic depiction of this idea is presented in Figure 2.1. Importantly, especially after the
development of the swampland program, it is expected that within the vast space of candidate
effective theories derived from string theory, those forming the space of low-energy effective
theories of quantum gravity occupy only a very tiny portion. To quantify this intuition, recall
that, as reviewed in the introduction, for models derived from type IIB string theory, estimates
as large as 10500 [27] have been made for the number of solutions. Such estimates not only
highlight the necessity of organizing principles within the space of string theory solutions, but
also foreshadow the difficulty in formulating such principles.

The expectation that not every effective theory can be utilized as a low-energy description of
quantum gravity is perhaps natural, but raises the question: how can we distinguish effective
theories in the landscape from those in the swampland? Within the swampland program this

• Conformal Field Theory Distance Conjecture [149]: All theories at infinite distance

Focusing on the second part of the swampland distance conjecture, a natural question that

• Emergent String Conjecture [153]: Any infinite distance limit in the moduli space of
a quantum gravity theory is either a decompactification limit, where the lightest tower
emerging corresponds to Kaluza-Klein modes, or an emergent string limit, where the
lightest tower is that of particle excitations of a unique weakly coupled, asymptotically
tensionless Type II or heterotic string, accompanied by a tower of Kaluza-Klein states
with the same mass scale.

The interpretation of the states as Kaluza-Klein modes and particular types of strings assumes
a suitable choice of duality frame in which these modes admit a weakly coupled interpretation.
Note that these statements refer to the lightest towers of states and not the entire light spectrum.
For example, one may consider a decompactification at weak string coupling where the lightest
towers would be Kaluza-Klein modes, with fundamental string modes being light, but heavier
than them.

Most evidence for this conjecture has been collected within string theory and M-theory com-
pactifications [154–167], but further supporting evidence has been collected from black hole
arguments [168, 169]. More recently, the emergent string conjecture has also been used to
argue for the existence of quantum obstructions to accessing certain infinite distance limits
in the moduli space [170–172]. We note that the proposed lower bound of the parameter λ
in (2.1) corresponds to an emergent string limit in d dimensions [101] and that the emergent
string conjecture has been used in deriving taxonomic rules for how different duality frames
can potentially be combined to gain a global understanding of the moduli space of string
compactifications [173].

Due to its relevance for the present thesis, we have so far focused on the swampland distance
conjecture and its potential refinements or extensions. It is important to note that not all
swampland conjectures fall into these two categories. In fact, we will present two additional
fundamental conjectures within this program, the weak gravity conjecture and the absence of
global symmetries conjecture.

2.1.3 The No Global Symmetries Conjecture

Let us finish our review of swampland conjectures with one that is arguably one of the pillars
of the swampland program, although it actually predates it. For earlier related references, see,
for example, [180–182].

• No Global Symmetries Conjecture (e.g. [183]): A theory coupled to gravity cannot
have any exact global symmetries.

The conjecture is typically supported both by black hole and holographic arguments. For a
review of both and related references we refer the interested reader to e.g. [184].

In order to achieve absence of global symmetries, one has two options: breaking the symmetry
by introducing an appropriate object, a symmetry-breaking defect ∆, or gauging it. Let us
briefly summarize what we mean by those two options. Assume we have a p-form global
symmetry and an associated (p+ 1)-form conserved current J satisfying

d ∗ J = 0 . (2.5)

Explicitly breaking the symmetry by a charged defect ∆ implies that the conservation law is
no longer satisfied

d ∗ J = δ(d−p)∆ ̸= 0 , (2.6)

while gauging it implies that we introduce an additional coupling in the action S of the form∫
B ∧ ∗J ⊂ S , (2.7)

where given that ∗J is a form of degree d−p−1 in d dimensions,B is a (p+1)-form. Promoting
B to a dynamical field gauges the symmetry. The corresponding conservation equation is then
modified by the equations of motion of the dynamical gauge field.

Applying the above conjecture implies that when encountering a global symmetry in an effective
field theory, one must either find an object responsible for its breaking or an appropriate gauge
field that may be coupled to it. It turns out that, although this is a simple line of reasoning,
its predictive power is limited, so a more fruitful approach has been to consider more general
notions of conserved charges, namely higher-form topological charges. In the context of the
swampland program, the topological charges of most interest are the ones corresponding to



Species Scale 55

so-called cobordism groups1, whose trivialization is predicted by the cobordism conjecture
[185]. This may be viewed as a tool to formalize the expectation that all consistent quantum
gravity backgrounds enjoy some sort of equivalence relation.

This line of research has been very successful in predicting and classifying objects in string
theory [186–190]. More recently, it has motivated the study of potential realizations of string
dualities as defects [189, 191–193]. We also note in passing the notion of dynamical cobordism,
which concerns curvature singularities located at finite spacetime distance and interprets the
potential appearance of certain scaling relations as evidence for the existence of end-of-the-
world objects predicted by the cobordism conjecture. This framework was originally introduced
in [194, 195].

Although this is by no means a complete list of conjectures, the reader has by now seen some of
the most widely used arguments and conjectures in the context of swampland applications. A
recurring theme has been the prediction of the appearance of new particles, typically organized
in towers, or extended objects. So far, very little has been said about how these degrees of
freedom affect the validity of the effective theory.

2.2 Species Scale

We have anticipated that the swampland distance conjecture [31] signifies a breakdown of the
effective field theory, but we have not yet quantified this statement. In quantum gravity appli-
cations, the ultraviolet cutoff, understood as the energy scale at which quantum gravitational
effects can no longer be considered suppressed, is typically referred to as the species scale [196,
197]. We will now proceed to review and contrast the various definitions and interpretations
of the species scale, before providing an additional interpretation of it in the context of the
Emergence Proposal in section 3.1. In that context, it will no longer be understood as a Wilso-
nian cutoff, but as the energy scale distinguishing between perturbative and non-perturbative
degrees of freedom.

model of particle physics, which is valid above that energy. The conclusion is thus that the

Taking into account the bounds imposed by the heating of neutron stars by surrounding clouds
of Kaluza-Klein gravitons yielded the most stringent bounds of the original analysis [228],
imposing that a single extra dimension is opening up at the micrometer scale, the so-called
dark dimension.3 In this case, the theory’s species scale is the five-dimensional Planck scale.

An appealing aspect of this scenario is that the Kaluza-Klein modes of the graviton can be
natural dark matter candidates [225, 231]. Primordial black holes [232] or axions [233] could
also play such a role. In fact, five-dimensional primordial black holes and a gas of massive
Kaluza–Klein gravitons were found to be equivalent [234]. In addition, the recent results of
the DESI collaboration [235, 236] indicate that the dark energy might be varying dynamically,
something that can be seen as a prediction of this scenario where the size of the single large
extra dimension evolves along its potential [237]. For reviews on the implications of this
proposal see e.g. [99, 238].

We would like to close this review of the dark dimension scenario by highlighting a related
paradox. Although the swampland principles used in its formulation are natural from a string-
theoretic point of view, a string-theoretic setup realizing the dark dimension scenario has
so far not been constructed in a controlled manner. See, however, [239–243] for concrete
top-down attempts and [244] for considerations related to its potential embedding in grand
unified theories, namely theories unifying gauge interactions in a single gauge group. Even
without a controlled top-down construction available, phenomenological aspects, such as the
interplay of neutrino masses and the cosmological constant in such a setup can be studied
[245].

Given that the predicted deviations from Newton’s law are investigated by various groups
(e.g. [246]), it remains to be seen whether this scenario will survive experimental tests and
what this will teach us about dark matter and quantum gravity!

2.4 The Emergence Proposal

So far quantum gravity has warned us that effective field theories at infinite geodesic distances
in the moduli space cannot be trusted due to the appearance of infinitely many light states
organized in towers by some typical mass gap. The lightest of these towers have been identified
by the emergent string conjecture and the energy at which the initial effective description
breaks down has been quantified by the species scale. In the previous discussion, however, the
species scale was not treated as a Wilsonian cutoff in the usual sense, since states saturating
the cutoff were still included, while no general prescription for integrating out states appearing
in towers was specified. The absence of exact global symmetries may also be understood as a
prediction of the existence of objects or couplings ensuring their breaking or gauging. What
remains lacking is a unified dynamical principle explaining the appearance of these towers and
their relation to the low-energy couplings.

3Nevertheless, see also [229, 230] for considerations of two large extra dimensions.



The Emergence Proposal 65

A bold conjecture aspiring to tackle these fundamental questions is the Emergence Proposal.
Before providing in section 3.1 a view of the Emergence Proposal in M-theory, we will review
the historical development of the concept in the context of quantum gravity and string theory.
Its original formulation (later referred to as strong version [204]) is based on earlier results
e.g [247–249] and states the following.

• Emergence Proposal [33]: The dynamics (kinetic terms) for all fields are emergent in
the infrared by integrating out towers down from an ultraviolet scale Λ, which is below
the Planck scale.

This is a simple statement with very deep consequences, since it is not restricted to quantum
corrections to a pre-existing term, as renormalization in particle physics would typically suggest.
Instead, it postulates that there is no kinetic term in the ultraviolet to begin with. Possible
interpretations for this reasoning are that the overarching ultraviolet theory is of topological

Moving beyond various forms of kinetic terms, the Emergence Proposal has also been applied

the entire low-energy effective action as emerging. This line of thought indicates that apart
from providing the dynamical interpretation of various statements we have encountered in
the context of the swampland program, the Emergence Proposal could potentially be a tool in
reconstructing various terms in the low-energy action by identifying the light spectrum of the
theory and integrating it out appropriately. Finally, the proposal seems to also resonate with
certain black hole results [210, 258, 259].

Let us summarize some of the central issues we have identified at the moment. The Emergence
Proposal is a deep statement about the effects of light states present in quantum gravity theories.
In the original formulation we have presented so far, it seems to face obstacles to being precisely
applied in both emergent string and decompactification limits, the only two possibilities allowed
by the emergent string conjecture. One could naively conclude that the only problem is that
this quantum field theory-inspired statement is simply not compatible with string modes. We
will argue that this conclusion is premature. Imposing a hard cutoff and restricting calculations
to states below that has been contested generally both in the context of gauge theories e.g. in
[260] (or more recently in [261] and in references therein) and in the context of quantum
gravitational applications e.g. [32, 262, 263].7 Additionally, it seems unlikely that modular
invariance can be reconciled with a truncation of towers, given the definitions of most modular
forms we have encountered so far in terms of infinite summations over the full Hilbert space
or at least full subsectors thereof.

7Moreover, also in the context of the Emergence Proposal itself, in footnote46 of [33], where the formulation
we have already presented appears as stated here, the necessity of integrating out the entire infinite towers is
implied. The applications in [248] are also compatible with this direction.



The Emergence Proposal 69

The next logical step would be to attempt to modify the original proposal. One avenue is
to try to weaken the original statement. Attempting to recover the modular dependence of
leading-order corrections to pre-existing tree-level terms in such a way (called weak emergence
in [204]) has been a very fruitful avenue on which most early applications of the proposal were
focused [33, 118, 151, 204, 253–257]. For more recent developments see also [167, 264–268].

However, since some of the obstructions already outlined affect also this more modest proposal
(see e.g. the gauge coupling considerations in [165]), we would like to focus on the original
(strong) formulation.

The remainder of the thesis is organized as follows:

• In section 3.1, we will introduce an M-theoretic refinement of the original Emergence
Proposal, also following the review [269]. We will shift our focus from subtleties of
other approaches to analogies with the development of string theory, drawing upon
the results of [270]. Concretely, after detecting the most appropriate M-theory limit
for the Emergence Proposal, we will identify as perturbative the states whose typical
mass scale is not above the species scale in that limit. Since the limit will correspond
to a decompactification of the M-theory circle with other compact volumes being fixed,
these particle states will be Kaluza-Klein modes and particles obtained from branes not
wrapping the M-theory circle. As we will see, a realization of our refinement also requires
the introduction of an appropriate regularization technique. We will review in detail
our chosen method, which has the advantage that it allows one to keep track of the
physical origin of the various contributions to amplitudes. It is based on Schwinger-like
integral representations and includes minimal subtraction and analytic continuation
of infinite sums. This scheme will be essential for providing concrete evidence for our
claims. We will shortly review its first application to a non-compact example in section
3.2, for which the prescription was originally developed, the resolved conifold. Besides
supporting our claims concerning the Emergence Proposal, this application fills a related
gap in the literature by extending the integrating-out interpretation of non-perturbative
contributions to the prepotential to the perturbative terms, at least for the resolved
conifold.

• Focusing on toroidal compactifications, we will turn our attention to a gravitational and a
gauge coupling, whose structure is intricately related to certain automorphic forms. The
structure of those forms is to a large extent understood from the point of view of U-duality,
which we will shortly review in section 4.1. We will then show that our logic suggests an
extension of the spectrum integrated out in computations for the R4-term in section 4.2
based on [271]. This extension will allow us to reproduce the full coupling in dimensions
d = 7, 8 and by decompactification in 9, 10, while admitting an interpretation in terms of
the properties of the related automorphic form, which is a constrained Eisenstein series,
in dimensions d ≥ 4. Turning the logic around, in section 4.3, we will apply the same
methods to a gauge coupling, the F 4-term in six dimensions, where we will exhibit the
redundancy of certain degrees of freedom, following [272]. The combination of the two
applications is compelling evidence that our proposed refinement identifies precisely the
relevant perturbative spectrum, without under- or overestimating it. They also serve as
extensive checks of our refinement and regularization procedure, which proved to be
compatible with the properties of these automorphic forms.





Part II

The Emergence Proposal in M-Theory





Chapter 3

An M-theoretic Refinement of Emergence

We will begin the main part of the present thesis by motivating an M-theoretic refinement of
the Emergence Proposal. Rather than focusing on the various obstacles already encountered,
we will follow a constructive approach, arguing that its central idea is compatible with funda-
mental aspects of string and M-theory, as well as aspects of particle physics, such as quantum
electrodynamics. We will then motivate the regularization technique used in our applications,
illustrating this prescription in the non-compact resolved conifold example in section 3.2.3.

3.1 Overview and Formulation of Refinement

The Emergence Proposal is a very attractive statement for a quantum gravity theory, as its
starting point is the expectation that geometry is a quantum effect. This seems unlikely to be
compatible with a typical perturbation theory, where one works with quantum corrections to a
pre-existing classical background. It is therefore expected that both a usual effective theory
prescription and perturbative string theory will be challenged by it.

We have already encountered a theory which, despite appearing in the framework of string
theory, is not captured by its perturbative expansion and in fact seems to require a completely
different treatment to be perturbatively quantized, M-theory. In what follows, we will propose
a refinement of the Emergence Proposal in M-theory. In doing so, we will provide a concrete
suggestion for which states are to be integrated out for the computation of observables, drawing
on lessons from string theory. Ultimately, such a proposal should be formulated in terms of the
fundamental degrees of freedom of M-theory and, ideally, should not rely on supersymmetry.
As a quantized perturbative theory of M-theory has not been formulated (yet), we will content
ourselves with statements at the level of type IIA objects and the corresponding particles
obtained from them. Note that to ease notation from now on we will denote MPl,11 =M∗.

• Emergence Proposal (M-theory) [269]: In the infinite distance limit to M-theory
M∗R11 ≫ 1, approached by keeping the d-dimensional Planck scale constant and com-
pactification cycles at order O(1) in eleven-dimensional Planck units M∗, a perturbative
quantum gravity theory arises whose low-energy effective description emerges via quan-
tum effects by integrating out the full infinite towers of states with a typical mass scale
parametrically not larger than the 11D Planck scale. These are Kaluza-Klein modes and
transversally wrapped M2- and M5-branes carrying momentum along the eleventh
direction.

Our proposal is that while the species scale remains relevant for the Emergence Proposal,

distance conjecture, we propose that any tower with a typical mass scale lying below or at
the species scale, the eleven dimensional Planck scale, is to be integrated out completely in
amplitudes. This includes individual states which are heavier than the species scale. Any tower
with mass scale above the species scale cannot be included in perturbative calculations. This is
similar to how in type II string theories on a compact background, although all string winding
modes would be considered, Dp-branes would not be included in a perturbative amplitude.

3.2.3 M-theoretic Emergence Proposal on the Resolved Conifold

The conifold plays an important role in the local description of compact Calabi-Yau manifolds
close to singularities. Zooming into the vicinity of the singularity leads to considering non-
compact Calabi-Yau spaces. Although gravity decouples in the strict non-compact limit of the
manifold8, they still exhibit interesting properties, for example through wrapped Dp-branes at
singularities.

Considering the standard complex coordinates {X,Y, U, V } on C4, the conifold is a singular
non-compact Calabi-Yau, which has a singularity at the origin. Locally, the vicinity of the
singularity is described by

XY − UV = 0 . (3.47)

details see e.g. [288] or Appendix A.3 for an analogous discussion of the K3 surface). These
two options give rise to the deformed and the resolved conifold. The latter is the geometry of
interest here.

Although the resolved conifold has been a conveniently simple setup to test our claims both for
the spectrum of light states required to obtain complete results via an integrating-out procedure

the limit ti → λti with λ → ∞ and i = 1, . . . , h1,1(Y ). With the four-dimensional dilaton
kept constant, this limit is equivalent to the decompactification limit to five dimensions of
M-theory on Y × S1.

The light particle degrees of freedom would now include D2-D0 bound states wrapping all
2-cycles in the homology latticeH2(Y,Z). Then, one must sum over them in the Schwinger-like
integral so that the result will be sensitive to all Kähler moduli ti. This means that the full
topological amplitude F1, including the linear terms, will emerge from a Schwinger one-loop

consider also contributions from BPS states involving NS5-branes and Kaluza-Klein modes
along Y . Determining their finite contributions requires a proper quantization of the wrapped
NS5-branes, which has so far been out of reach. Moreover, the general Schwinger integral
(3.40) contains contributions from the r = 1 sector, associated with genus 1 curves in Y . Such
states contribute to Fg for g ≥ 1.

Significant progress has been achieved in extending this computation to the quintic and several
further Calabi-Yau examples. This included a regularization of the sums over Gopakumar-Vafa
invariants required for computing triple intersection numbers appearing in F0 as emergent via
an integrating-out procedure in the suggested M-theory limit [322]. This result was further
elaborated on in [323], where the same methodology was also applied to F1. Naturally, one
would like to consider increasingly more complicated setups and different couplings, however
this is of significant computational difficulty. For instance, an Emergence Proposal-inspired
integrating-out procedure has to this day not yet been applied in the context of Calabi-Yau
fourfolds although their enumerative geometry contains invariants of similar structure [324].
We further note that in [264–266], analytic continuation of the integrals to complex proper
time was suggested for the study of non-perturbative results, in a sense in the same spirit as
our discussion of electron pair production.

Before considering further applications of the M-theoretic Emergence Proposal, let us address

Chapter 4

M-theoretic Emergence and Eisenstein Series

In this chapter, we will consider applications of the M-theoretic Emergence Proposal in compact-
ifications with maximal and half-maximal supersymmetry. Although section 4.2 will concern a
gravitational coupling, theR4-term, and section 4.3 will concern a gauge coupling, the F 4-term,
the mathematical structure of the two amplitudes is in fact quite similar and related to the
structure of U-duality groups. For this reason, we will begin with some mathematical prelimi-
naries, before proceeding to the main results, which will rely on their integral representations
in terms of Schwinger-like integrals, to which our previously outlined methodology will be
applied. We assume the reader is familiar with aspects of representation theory.

From a physical perspective, for the R4-term our refinement will suggest an extension of the
integrated-out spectrum of light particle states appearing in its computations, while for the
F 4-term a reduction thereof. Given these two complementary results, this chapter provides
substantial evidence that our prescription correctly identifies the perturbative particle states in
the M-theory limit of interest. It also illustrates the power of our regularization scheme, which
allows working with expansions making the properties of the corresponding automorphic
forms evident.

4.1 U-duality and Eisenstein Series

Let us consider M-theory compactified on a torus Tn. We have already discussed that such
a compactification would preserve maximal supersymmetry and encountered a symmetry of
this theory when viewed as the strongly coupled limit of type IIA on Tn−1, which is T-duality.
It turns out that the quantum symmetry of such a setup is actually U-duality [330], some
properties of which we will review here, mainly following [191, 331].

In order to identify the quantum symmetries of a theory, one needs to consider not only the
low-energy effective action, but also the spectrum. More concretely, by compactifying type
IIA string theory on Tn−1, one might naively expect that this theory is symmetric under
O(n− 1, n− 1,R) by considering momentum and winding modes classically. If one, however,
takes into account that momentum and winding are quantized and that the determinant-(−1)
elements of O(n, n,Z) flip chirality, therefore exchanging the theory to type IIB as we have
seen, one would consider SO(n− 1, n− 1,Z) as the appropriate T-duality group. However,
this would not necessarily be the correct quantum symmetry if it did not preserve the lattice of
Dp-brane charges, which it does.

BPS condition (4.26) can be treated as solving a linear Diophantine equation in k ≥ 3 variables

As reviewed in Appendix D, solving a linear Diophantine equation in k variables requires the
introduction of k − 1 integers for the Kaluza-Klein momenta mI . This corresponds to the
situation in which all k winding numbers are non-vanishing. Setting any winding number
to zero leads to the corresponding Kaluza-Klein momentum being unconstrained, so that we

of vanishing nI as described by a vector α, the only exception being the case in which all of
them are vanishing as there is no Diophantine equation to be solved anymore. Physically,
this corresponds to the pure Kaluza-Klein sector of the computation. We will not consider
this sector in what follows, but rather assume that at least one of the winding numbers is
non-vanishing. We will now show that the constant contribution, 2π2/3, is related to extended
objects, in this case strings, a point that will also be crucial for our M-theoretic implications.

space-time instantons. From the discussion in the previous sections, we found the corre-
spondence between particles in the loop and instantons as summarized in Table 4.7. Here
e.g. (D0,KK(K)) means that we focus on this contribution to (4.131), perform a Poisson re-
summation on the Kaluza-Klein mode in the K-direction and apply the formula (4.39). The
argument of the Bessel functions allows us to read off the corresponding instanton action.
This shows in particular that even though we are not integrating out particle states resulting
from wrapped fundamental strings or D4-branes, i.e. longitudinal M2- and M5-branes, their
instantons are nevertheless arising from integrating out transverse M2- and M5-branes. Note
that a different regularization method, would possibly obstruct a direct mapping between
integrated-out states and physical contributions, but could still yield the correct result.

To conclude the discussion of the R4-coupling, we point out that a systematic analysis of
infinite-distance limits throughout the eight-dimensional toroidal moduli space, together with
selected seven-dimensional limits, was carried out in [355]. This confirmed that an emergence-
like prescription gives rise to the full results only in our M-theory limit. The instantonic
spectrum that can be obtained by an integrating-out procedure in various limits was identified
in the same work, giving rise to a notion of taxonomic rules along the lines of [173].

Conclusions and Outlook

Let us conclude by summarizing our findings and what we have learned about the role of
emergence in the swampland program and M-theory.

In the present thesis, we focused on a particular realization of the concept of emergence,
as originally inspired by the Emergence Proposal, formulated within the framework of the
swampland program. The original proposal postulated that kinetic terms could be derived as
quantum effects via an integrating-out procedure, however it was later interpreted as not being
solely restricted to kinetic terms.

Our goal was to refine this notion into a version that could recover complete results, rather
than leading-order estimates of corrections to pre-existing terms. This was realized in perhaps
one of the most surprising corners of the string theory framework, M-theory. We identified
an isotropic decompactification limit to this eleven-dimensional theory as the most relevant
for extracting maximum information from amplitudes in an integrating-out manner, while
providing a concrete regularization algorithm to perform these calculations. In that case,
although the eleventh direction was decompactifying, all other compact directions were kept
fixed in M-theory units. This implied that only Kaluza-Klein modes and branes not wrapping
the large eleventh direction would become light when approaching the decompactification
limit.

Our motivation for how to work with the spectrum identified as light and therefore perturbative
relied heavily on string-theoretic amplitudes, rather than the Wilsonian approach to effective
field theories. This implied that the quantum gravity cutoff, the species scale, which in this case
was the eleven-dimensional Planck scale, was understood as characterizing towers appearing at
the asymptotics of the moduli space as perturbative or not and not as a hard cutoff. Concretely,
entire particle towers were being integrated out, rather than being truncated at some energy
level.

On a conceptual level, we explored how our refinement appears, in our opinion, as compatible
with the physical structure of M-theory and how it may also be used as inspiration to extract
more information regarding its potential perturbative quantization, which still lies beyond
current techniques. In doing so, we commented on how our ideas regarding the fact that
M2- and M5- branes should be considered on equal footing conceptually interplay with
membrane physics, conformal field theories, matrix models etc. On a technical level, we
followed a pragmatic approach of calculating supersymmetrically protected amplitudes using
only the light particle spectrum obtained by wrapping the corresponding light branes on
compact directions. As a first application, we verified that our refinement and regularization
prescription can give rise to the full results for the prepotential of the resolved conifold. These
importantly included also the (unambiguous) perturbative terms. The last part of the thesis
was focusing on toroidal compactifications, examining a gravitational and a gauge coupling



156 Conclusions and Outlook

whose mathematical structure was found to be compatible with our M-theoretic Emergence
Proposal in a highly non-trivial manner.

Our prescription suggested an extension of the integrated-out spectrum for the R4-coupling in
toroidal compactifications of M-theory compared to previous attempts to describe it via super-
gravity calculations focusing only on Kaluza-Klein modes. It was verified that the extension
to light particles obtained from M2- and M5-branes wrapping compact cycles but not the
M-theory circle produces the complete results expected from string-theoretic amplitudes down
to 7D, while we argued that we expect the result to hold up to 4D. To achieve this, we examined
the expected instanton spectrum and analyzed how our findings are compatible with more
formal conjectures relating the amplitude to constrained Eisenstein series of maximal parabolic
subgroups of U-duality groups in dimensions down to 4D. Contributions not reproduced directly
were related to the presence of extended objects and obtained systematically in the decompact-
ification limits of lower-dimensional results. For an F 4-gauge coupling in 6D heterotic/type
IIA theories, our refinement of the Emergence Proposal proposed a reduction of the spectrum
of states contributing to the amplitude, which we verified through the cancellations of heavy,
from our point of view non-perturbative, contributions of M5-branes also wrapping the large
eleventh direction. Similar to the computations for the R4-term, although we were considering
the light spectrum in our decompactification limit, the results were exact. In both cases, the
analysis was performed in rectangular tori, but we expect the results to remain valid upon
including non-trivial Kalb-Ramond fields.

The applications presented in this thesis provide strong indications that we have managed to
identify the precise fundamental particle spectrum for these protected couplings in M-theory
compactifications in our proposed limit, not a sub- or superset. Hence, we have encountered
an instance where the swampland program has motivated a new look at established aspects of
string-theoretic calculations. Our developed regularization scheme, which included minimal
subtraction and analytic continuation, was crucial in keeping track of the physical origin
of the various contributions appearing in Schwinger-like integrals describing the examined
amplitudes. Such a scheme would not have been available if we had insisted on treating the
species scale as a strict cutoff.

Nevertheless, we view these results as the beginning rather than the end of the story. On a
realistic level, our checks had to begin from well-controlled setups, which is why we focused on
supersymmetrically protected terms that were not receiving perturbative corrections beyond
one loop. This restriction to protected observables is natural, since our limit does not lie in
a parametrically controlled eleven-dimensional supergravity regime, making quantities with
strong non-renormalization properties particularly valuable probes. Although even then the
resulting expressions were convoluted, highlighting the non-triviality of our regularization
prescription, in the future one would need to consider further extensions to more generic
terms. Additionally, recalling that the initial motivation for the Emergence Proposal was also
to provide a tool to derive other swampland constraints, it would be interesting to revisit how
this can happen at least in our limit of interest, for example for some versions of the weak
gravity conjecture.

Let us provide some examples of the impact of the presented results. In the context of phe-
nomenology, recently, we presented a very bold application of the Emergence Proposal, in
which the limit of interest to us throughout this thesis was related to the Dark Dimension



Conclusions and Outlook 157

Scenario [360], thus relating our considerations to phenomenology. Although this application
is highly speculative, it also highlights that, at least at the moment, our refinement stands
as one of the few remaining candidates for performing perturbative calculations, or at least
estimates thereof, in an intrinsically M-theoretic regime. The ultimate goal would be, of course,
to reformulate the conjecture purely in terms of M-theoretic degrees of freedom, letting go of
the type IIA intuition, and use it as a building tool for the corresponding theory. Due to the
lack of a microscopic description of M-theory, this remains a formidable task. In that context,
on a conceptual level, the works presented in this thesis motivated revisiting the BFSS matrix
model and exploring potential M5-brane extensions thereof without changing the theory’s
background [277].

We therefore propose to view the present thesis as a detailed invitation to reconsider what
information about M-theory is within our reach. From its potential applications in the swamp-
land program or phenomenology to formal aspects of membrane quantization, it clearly has
many lessons waiting to emerge!

A.3 K3 surface

A K3 surface1 is the only compact Calabi-Yau two-fold with SU(2) holonomy. In fact, it is a
theorem that any two K3 surfaces are diffeomorphic to each other. For physical applications
one often considers K3 as a toroidal orbifold. To achieve this, one considers a 4-torus, which
can be understood as a two-dimensional complex manifold by quotienting the complex plane
C2, with coordinates (z1, z2) by the group Z4, generated by

zi → zi + 1 , zj → zj + i , i = 1, 2 . (A.22)

One then considers the Z2 group of isometries generated by (z1, z2)→ (−z1,−z2), which has
16 fixed points. The identifications described above imply that the previously non-contractible
loops of the torus may now be shrunk to a point, thus trivializing its fundamental group
π1(T

4/Z2). Additionally, the holomorphic 2-form dz1 ∧ dz2 is invariant under the Z2 action
and the same holds for the complex structure and the Kähler form, so we can identify it with
the orbifold limit of a K3 surface.

1We note the fun fact that although the name K3 is typically related to Kummer, Kähler and Kodaira, with physics
literature sometimes referring to K3 as Kummer’s third surface, the name is believed to be inspired by the
numbering of peaks of the Karakorum mountain range.

To consider this space as a manifold, one needs to make it smooth, which can be achieved by a
procedure called blowing-up the singularities. This is a local procedure so one can focus at a
patch of the orbifold. The space C2/Z2 can be embedded to C3 by considering the coordinates
(x0, x1, x2) and the hypersurface A given by

This is smooth everywhere apart from the origin where it is singular. This can be further
parametrized in a Z2-invariant way, by considering x0 = ξ2, x1 = η2 and x2 = ξη. One sees

By fixing a point in P2, we fix a line in C3, while fixing a point in C3 determines a point in P2,

to as a blow-up of C3 at the origin. The P2 which has “grown" out of the origin is called the
exceptional divisor.

Consider a path in A towards the origin. In the blow-up, the exact point on the exceptional
divisor we find depends on the angle from which the origin is approached. It turns out that the
singularity is replaced by a P1 ≃ S2, thus rendering the space smooth. If all 16 fixed points of

Linear Diophantine Equations

Diophantine equations are polynomial equations with integer coefficients and for which one
is interested in integer solutions. They owe their name to the mathematician Diophantus of
Alexandria, who first studied them in the 3rd century. Despite the fact that they have been
continuously studied since then, it was only in the 20th century that it was proved that there
is no general algorithm determining whether an arbitrary Diophantine equation admits an
integer solution. This is the content of the MRDP theorem, named after the authors’ initials
[369], motivated by Hilbert’s tenth problem in mathematics. Fortunately, the situation is under
control for linear Diophantine equations. Since quadratic BPS conditions (e.g. (4.4)) appearing
in our analysis can be treated as such in our computations, in this appendix we present a brief
overview of linear Diophantine equations and how to solve them. More information can be
found, for example, in the classic reference [370].

The simplest instance is a linear Diophantine equation in two variables,X and Y , of the form

aX + bY = c, a, b, c ∈ Z, a or b ̸= 0. (D.1)

It is a theorem (e.g. Theorem 1, chapter 5 of [370]) that this equation admits integer solutions
iff gcd(a, b) divides c. If c = 0, the general solution is X = Nb, Y = −Na with N ∈ Z. If
c ̸= 0, the general solution is

X = X0 +Nb , Y = Y0 −Na , (D.2)

where (X0, Y0) is any solution of (D.1). Notice that one can assume gcd(a, b) = 1 from the
start without loss of generality. Indeed, if this condition is not met, one can divide (D.1) by
g2 ≡ gcd(a, b) > 1 to get ãX + b̃Y = c̃, with ã = a/g2 and similarly for b̃, c̃ and recover
again a linear Diophantine equation with coprime coefficients. The solution in the case g2 > 1
is given by replacing a → a/g2 and b → b/g2 in (D.2). Since this observation is valid for
any number of variables, we will systematically start with coprime coefficients. Knowing the
solution to the linear Diophantine equation in two variables, one can iterate the algorithm and
solve linear Diophantine equations in more variables.

abstracts.value: We give a polynomial-time randomized classical algorithm that approximates the largest eigenvalue $λ_{\max}$ of a traceless quartic fermionic Hamiltonian $H$ on $n$ modes. The algorithm achieves energy at least $λ_{\max}/O(\sqrt n)$ and outputs either a fermionic Gaussian state or a polynomially sparse state in the Fock basis. This is achieved through a new upper bound on $λ_{\max}$ in terms of the maximum energy of a Gaussian state and $\sqrt{2^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}(H^2)}$.

titles.title: Improved classical optimization of fermionic Hamiltonians beyond Gaussian states

abstracts.value: Quantum compilers play a critical role in transforming high-level quantum programs into optimized, hardware-compatible circuits. However, verifying the correctness of compiler passes remains challenging, as determining the expected output of large, deeply entangled quantum circuits is computationally intractable. This challenge is further amplified when compiler passes modify already complex circuit structures, making manual validation of transformed circuits impractical. In this work, we perform a systematic analysis of unit tests for quantum compiler passes in four quantum programming frameworks (PennyLane, Qiskit, Cirq, and pytket). Our findings indicate validation is dominated by program-content and program-metric assertions, and test circuits are generally small and shallow. Motivated by these observations, we introduce a testing methodology for automated validation of quantum compiler passes based on retromorphic testing and principles from the Hadamard test. This methodology analyzes a compiler pass, test circuit, and expected pass behavior to verify semantic preservation and intended structural modifications. We implement our methods in a framework, RetroQ, and apply it to compiler passes in PennyLane and Qiskit. Experimental evaluation reproduced several existing bugs as well as uncovered previously undetected defects, such as flawed symbolic parameter handling, incorrect commutation logic, failure to recognize self-adjointness of gates, and runtime crashes. These findings highlight the need for compiler-pass-specific testing methodologies to improve the reliability of the evolving quantum software stack.

titles.title: Retromorphic Testing of Quantum Compiler Passes

abstracts.value: Variational quantum algorithms are often limited by barren plateaus: gradients vanish as circuit size and depth increase, making quantum neural networks difficult to train. We propose Q-Capsule, a localized capsule-based quantum neural architecture that mitigates this problem through register partitioning, local readout, sparse inter-capsule coupling, trainable data re-uploading, and Quantum Fisher Information Matrix (QFIM)-guided adaptive depth growth. By restricting the dominant support of each observable to a small capsule and controlling inter-capsule entanglement, Q-Capsule preserves useful gradient signals while retaining communication between local quantum representations. As the register width increases, Q-Capsule consistently maintains stable gradient variance, whereas globally entangling baselines exhibit exponential suppression with a log-gradient-variance slope near -ln 2 per qubit. Q-Capsule also produces more structured optimization landscapes, higher parameter efficiency, improved robustness to depolarizing noise, and lower measurement requirements. Its adaptive policy achieves 98.1% accuracy on binary classification and 97.7% on four-class classification, while using approximately 73% fewer two-qubit gates than the fixed-deep model on the multiclass task.

titles.title: Q-Capsule: A Localized Capsule-Based Quantum Neural Architecture for Barren Plateau Mitigation

abstracts.value: Multi-photon interference is the resource most native to photonic quantum machine learning, yet experiments on photonic reservoirs have reported advantages, null results, and train-only effects. These outcomes cannot be compared: each measures task-dependent accuracy on different tasks and platforms. Here we resolve the question task-independently through the kernel geometry of boson-sampling feature maps. Interference redistributes feature variance across roughly twice as many effective dimensions as distinguishable-particle statistics, generating a large geometric separation between the corresponding kernels. The separation grows superlinearly with indistinguishability, is linear in Hong--Ou--Mandel visibility at small visibility for two to four photons, and retains approximately 80% of its magnitude at the source quality of current quantum processors. Under experimental sampling budgets the separation is learnable on adversarially constructed tasks (accuracy advantage +0.22 plus or minus 0.05) and an order of magnitude smaller on natural tasks, gated by kernel--task alignment. The results reconcile the existing experimental record and supply a pre-experimental protocol: kernel geometry establishes that an interference-specific learning resource exists, and task alignment determines whether a given task can access it; both are computable before committing significant hardware resources.

titles.title: When Does Interference Help Learning? Kernel Geometry as a Pre-Experimental Test for Photonic Reservoir Computing

abstracts.value: We study a strong form of genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL), where an $n$-partite scenario admits a quantum strategy generating outcomes belonging to a restricted set with certainty, whereas every strategy built from nonclassical resources shared among at most $k<n$ parties fails this criterion with positive probability. This generalizes what is referred to as strong contextuality/nonlocality, or pseudotelepathy, beyond ruling out local models. For the simplest five-party Bell scenario of two binary-outcome measurement settings per party, we use the inflation technique to demonstrate that a game with a perfect quantum strategy witnesses a robust separation from models built from bipartite resources under local operations and shared randomness (LOSR), establishing the behavior is LOSR-GMNL. We provide broader context for this result by investigating its simulability with resources shared among three or four parties under different resource models and alternative definitions of GMNL. A central open question is whether $n$-party quantum resources can achieve such a separation from models built from $(n-1)$-party resources, for $n\ge 3$. We make progress here by constructing a family of robustly LOSR-GMNL games with $ε$-optimal quantum strategies experimentally indistinguishable in the limit from true probability-one-winning strategies for any desired level of precision.

titles.title: Minimal Scenarios Witnessing Genuine Multipartite Nonlocality Possibilistically

abstracts.value: Near-term quantum approaches to combinatorial optimization are limited by qubit counts, circuit fidelity, sampling cost, and the difficulty of encoding constraints, while machine learning is increasingly used to configure and control quantum optimization workflows. We call such workflows adaptive: decisions conventionally fixed in advance, from formulation and penalties to shot budgets, backends, and whether to invoke a quantum processor at all, are made by learned policies that respond to the instance, the progress of the solve, or the hardware. This review examines three paradigms, AI for quantum optimization, quantum for AI-driven optimization, and AI-quantum co-optimization, and organizes the literature by the decision being learned rather than by application. A structured search identified a 119-paper corpus, of which 67 papers form an evidence core coded in detail. The evidence is considerably stronger for AI-assisted quantum optimization than for the reverse direction: learning already reduces quantum evaluations, improves initialization, supports decomposition and penalty control, and mitigates noise, whereas evidence that quantum computation improves learned optimizers remains largely confined to small-scale simulation. Experimental controls are thin: of 52 studies in the three paradigms, 22 include no classical baseline, the quantum contribution is fully isolated in 10 of 24 where an ablation applies, and the median largest experiment uses 16 qubits. We introduce an M0-M5 evidence hierarchy, from simulation to practical quantum advantage, and find no broadly convincing result at the highest level. We argue that scaling is increasingly a systems problem: the question is not only whether a problem fits on a quantum processor, but how classical and quantum resources should be allocated across the optimization process.

titles.title: Beyond QAOA: A Review of AI and Quantum Computing for Adaptive Combinatorial Optimization

abstracts.value: Structural measures such as the clustering coefficient and the average shortest-path length characterise how a network is organised. These measures are typically formulated for real, non-negative edge weights. A class of quantum and photonic architectures has complex edge weights instead, whose phases determine whether alternative routes interfere constructively or destructively. These architectures are also bipartite, so triangles are absent and the smallest closed cycle is a four-node square. Existing measures address complex weights and bipartite structure separately: bipartite clustering coefficients quantify clustering through four-node squares but do not contain phase information, while interferometric coefficients retain phase but are defined on triangles. In this work, we define a clustering coefficient for complex-weighted bipartite networks which reduces to the classical bipartite coefficient when the phases vanish, becomes negative when alternative routes cancel, and can be obtained for all nodes from a single sparse matrix product. We show that the phase accumulated around a square is the smallest gauge-invariant carrier of structural phase information in a bipartite network. The clustering coefficient factorises into a topological contribution and a phase contribution, making a bipartite Watts--Strogatz ensemble analytically tractable. For phases uniformly distributed on $[-Δ,Δ]$, the mean phase contribution is $(\sinΔ/Δ)^4$, independent of node, degree, and topology. We also derive closed-form expressions for the clustering coefficient, open-path visibility, and phase variance. We numerically verify these predictions and further show that phase disorder increases coherent distance.

titles.title: A Gauge-Invariant Clustering Coefficient for Complex-Weighted Bipartite Networks

abstracts.value: Quantum networking represents the future of secure communication, enabling fundamentally new capabilities through quantum information exchange. However, these networks require secure, high-fidelity quantum communication channels, and they require every participating node to be a genuine quantum device. Currently, there is no reliable method to verify whether clients entering a quantum network truly possess quantum computational capability and are connecting over robust channels. In this work, we introduce a client-validation protocol that functions as a proof-of-quantum-capability handshake. Our protocol secures a quantum network against classical spoofers, noisy quantum computers, and genuine quantum devices connecting with the network over noisy or insecure channels. We validate the efficacy of this protocol through numerical simulations under erasure, dephasing, and depolarizing noise models.

titles.title: Secure Quantum Handshakes: Quantum Network Verification Via Simon's Algorithm

abstracts.value: Flow models generate trajectories from an initial distribution to a target distribution by solving an ordinary differential equation defined by a velocity field. Flow matching learns this velocity field by modeling the transport dynamics between the two distributions. Wavefunction flow establishes a formal connection between flow models and quantum dynamics by introducing a continuity Hamiltonian, which drives the Schrödinger evolution of quantum states. In this paper, we investigate accurate and efficient quantum simulation of the wavefunction flow, thereby realizing the efficient implementation of flow models on quantum computers. We first leverage a quantum read-only memory (QROM)-based phase kickback framework for the wavefunction flow simulation, generating probability densities that closely match those produced by the corresponding conventional flow model. To address the high circuit-resource cost, we further incorporate a trained quantum neural network (QNN) into the phase kickback framework, replacing QROM for data encoding. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our proposed method implements flow models on quantum computers more efficiently, since it maintains the accuracy of wavefunction flow simulation compared with the QROM-based framework, and significantly reduces the circuit resources.

titles.title: An Efficient Quantum Circuit for Flow Model Execution Using Quantum Neural Networks

abstracts.value: Quantum machine learning, and quantum neural networks (QNNs) in particular, are advancing fields with growing potential. Although systematic comparisons of QNN configurations have been explored primarily for classification tasks, comparatively little attention has been given to regression problems, particularly financial time series forecasting. This study presents a large-scale systematic comparative evaluation of QNN component configurations for financial time series forecasting, using the GBP/USD spot exchange rate as a case study. A grid search across encoding methods, ansatz designs, qubit counts, layer depths, and cost functions yields 1,368 distinct model configurations, each evaluated in terms of prediction accuracy, computational cost, and convergence behaviour. The results reveal unique insights into how the choice of methods influences performance, such as that gate selection and arrangement are more critical to model success than raw parameter count, and that entanglement is a system-level property of the full circuit rather than solely at the ansatz level. The best-performing QNN configuration achieves an $R^2$ score of 0.985, outperforming a classical BiLSTM baseline. Additionally, the impact of real quantum hardware noise is assessed through execution on the IQM Emerald device, revealing that gate errors and decoherence represent a significant barrier to practical deployment, with gate selection and circuit depth identified as key determinants of hardware noise resilience. Overall, the findings provide practical architectural guidance for QNN design and establish a baseline characterisation of QNN noise sensitivity on near-term quantum devices.

titles.title: Large-Scale Benchmarking of Quantum Neural Network Configurations for Financial Time Series Forecasting

abstracts.value: Machine learning (ML) in high-energy nuclear physics (HENP) is entering a new stage in which physical knowledge is incorporated more directly into data analysis, simulation, and physics inference. This mini-review focuses on developments that have matured in the past several years. Whereas earlier applications emphasized event classification, pattern recognition, and surrogate models for selected observables, recent work has moved toward physics-integrated workflows: calibrated Bayesian extraction of QCD matter properties, dense-matter equation-of-state inference from heavy-ion and neutron-star data, generative event modeling, neural unfolding of weak physical signals, differentiable inverse solvers, gauge-equivariant and diffusion-based lattice-field samplers, and neural reconstruction of model functions in holographic QCD. We survey recent applications of ML in heavy-ion collisions, neutron-star physics, lattice QFT, and holographic or continuum QCD. The emphasis is not on ML architectures alone, but on how they enter concrete physics workflows, how physical constraints such as symmetries, conservation laws, causality, thermodynamic stability, and topology are imposed, and how uncertainty quantification and validation determine whether an AI-assisted result can support a reliable physics conclusion.

titles.title: Machine Learning Meets High-Energy Nuclear Physics: From Pattern Recognition to Physics-Integrated Discovery

abstracts.value: We study two problems: Local Leakage Resilience (LLR) for Shamir secret sharing, and worst-case Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI). Both problems concern polynomials $Q(X)$ of degree less than $k$, over a prime-order finite field $\mathbb{F}_p$. In LLR for Shamir secret sharing, one asks how much one can learn about $Q(0)$ given a few bits leaked from each of $Q(α_1), \ldots, Q(α_n)$, for distinct non-zero evaluation points $α_i \in \mathbb{F}_p$. In OPI, one is given input list $S_1, \ldots, S_n \subset \mathbb{F}_p$, and wants to find a polynomial $Q(X)$ of degree less than $k$ so that $Q(α_i) \in S_i$ for as many $i$ as possible. Leveraging recent connection between these two problems due to (Sun, Wootters 2026), we improve the state-of-the-art for both problems. For LLR, we show that there is some constant $δ> 0$ so that, as long as $R := k/n \geq 1/2 - δ$, Shamir secret-sharing is one-bit locally leakage resilient (meaning that one can learn only a negligible amount about $Q(0)$). This is the first result to break the so-called "one-half barrier" for LLR, and improves over the previous best known result, requiring $R \geq 0.668$ (Kasser, 2025). For OPI, we give a quantum algorithm that finds a polynomial $Q(X)$ that agrees with at least a $\mathsf{SCL}_ρ(R)-\varepsilon$ fraction of the lists in expectation, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, where $\mathsf{SCL}_ρ$ is the \emph{semicircle law} of (Jordan et al., 2025). This improves previous algorithmic (and existential) results of (Jo, 2026) and (Horinaga, Yamakawa, 2026). We also give further improved existential results. abstracts.value: Large-scale Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) networks rely on trusted repeaters, making the security properties of the selected communication path an essential part of end-to-end assurance. At the same time, network operators may be unwilling to disclose their internal topology. We present a topology-certification mechanism that lets a provider prove in zero knowledge that policy-compliant routes between two endpoints exist, without disclosing the routes in an individual presentation. Our main idea is to certify nodes and edges independently using multi-message signatures, rather than signing the complete graph as one object. For a route chosen in advance, proof size and cryptographic proving and verification work depend on its positions and attributes, independently of the overall network size, whereas route discovery and certification have separate graph-dependent costs. The construction hides the actual route length up to a public bound and sketches extensions to node-disjoint routes and monotonic additions within a graph epoch. We give a formal security model and conditional proofs of unforgeability and graph hiding for a generic construction. For a BBS-based construction, presentation-size estimates remain below $300$ KiB at $\ell=m=n=50$, and measured generation and verification times remain below $400$ ms at $\ell=64$ and $m=n=8$.

titles.title: Certifying Hidden Paths: Scalable Topology Assurance for QKD Networks

abstracts.value: Building a quantum model involves a tradeoff: how complex the circuit should be, and how much training data it needs. Caro et al. show that models with fewer trainable gates need less training data to generalize well. Q-FLAIR shows that a quantum feature-map circuit can be grown gate-by-gate, stopping once further growth stops improving the training loss. We ask whether these two results combine into a predictable scaling law. Does Q-FLAIR's own stopping rule pick larger or smaller circuits as training data grows? Does the resulting generalization behavior track Caro et al.'s bound? We reimplement Q-FLAIR's growth mechanism faithfully, including its analytic reconstruction and exact stopping rule. We run it on full-resolution (784-pixel) MNIST 3-vs-5 classification, at five training-set sizes from N = 2000 to 10000. We then fine-tune each resulting circuit, so we can measure Caro et al.'s notion of active gates, K. We find no predictable relationship between training-set size and the circuit size Q-FLAIR converges to. Circuit size and test accuracy both vary non-monotonically with N, and seed-to-seed variance is nearly as large as any trend across N. The empirical generalization gap never exceeds Caro et al.'s bound in 14 of 15 runs, so the bound holds as a valid guarantee in those runs. But the gap correlates only weakly with the bound's value (r = 0.12). This shows that K does not explain most of the variation we observe. Why a valid guarantee can coexist with such weak predictive power remains an open question, and answering it may be necessary before circuit depth and training data size can be jointly optimized in practice.

titles.title: Toward Joint Optimization of Circuit Depth and Training Data Size in Adaptively Grown Quantum Classifiers

abstracts.value: We present a non-perturbative formulation of quantum gravity in asymptotically flat spacetimes using Witten's cubic open string field theory (OSFT) on unstable D-branes. Given that the massless spin-2 sector of the closed string spectrum inherently encodes the degrees of freedom of quantum gravity, we establish this connection by mapping on-shell closed string excitations directly to gauge-invariant operators in OSFT, realizing a concrete flat-space analogue of the AdS/CFT correspondence. By evaluating the OSFT correlation functions of these operators perturbatively around the tachyon vacuum, we systematically reproduce the all-orders genus expansion of the closed string S-matrix for the associated states. This demonstrates that closed string theory-and thus quantum gravity-emerges dynamically from the open string tachyon vacuum, establishing Witten's OSFT as a fully calculable, non-perturbative framework for flat-space quantum gravity.

abstracts.value: We present a spacetime that serves as a horizonless mimicker of extremal black holes. Unlike previously studied mimickers of black holes with non-degenerate horizons, whose geometries are of the wormhole type and consist of two asymptotically flat regions connected by a very long throat, the mimicker of an extremal black hole possesses a single asymptotically flat region at one end and an infinitely long throat at the other. In the throat region, the spacetime approaches the direct-product geometry $M_{1,1} \times S^2$, where $M_{1,1}$ is two-dimensional Minkowski spacetime and $S^2$ is the two-sphere. We investigate scalar-field dynamics and the fate of the Aretakis instability. Although Aretakis-like modes arise in a local analysis of the throat, they do not lead to a physical instability of the mimicker. A scalar perturbation initially localized in the throat gives rise, at late times, to a sequence of signals with a characteristic separation $t_{\rm delay}\sim 1/λ$, where $λ\ll 1$ is a deformation parameter. This timescale is parametrically larger than the echo time $t_{\rm echo}\sim \ln(1/λ)$ characteristic of non-extremal black-hole mimickers. We refer to this sequence as a {\it long-delay signal train}. Geometrically, the periodicity of the long-delay signals is associated with periodic geodesics on $S^2$. We then extend the construction to extremal Kerr. In this case, the throat region approaches a generalized product geometry involving $M_{1,1}$ and a two-dimensional surface $Σ_2$. The corresponding signals are expected to form a quasi-periodic signal train, reflecting the quasi-periodic geodesic motion on $Σ_2$. We also comment on the generalization to wormhole mimickers of non-extremal black holes and on the implications of these results for unitarity in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence.

titles.title: Extremal black hole mimickers: geometry, stability, and long-delay signal trains

abstracts.value: Using notions from graded Poisson geometry, we develop a framework that allows for concise formulations of field theories such as Einstein-Cartan and Palatini-Cartan gravity. abstracts.value: Trapped-ion quantum simulators are powerful platforms for exploring many-body physics, yet engineering of arbitrary interaction graphs remains a central challenge. To leverage the intrinsic structure of native motional modes and thereby enhance programmability, a residual-guided optimization protocol is introduced for the systematic design of multi-tone global drive spectra. While the achievable interaction fidelity is fundamentally bounded by the available motional modes, this adaptive strategy converges on the theoretical limit using a number of laser tones that scales nearly linearly with system size. The versatility of this method enables the synthesis of both long-range and traditionally difficult short-range coupling topologies. Additionally, by incorporating a penalty for residual motional excitation, the algorithm effectively mitigates errors associated with incomplete closure of phase-space trajectories. Overall, this scalable framework significantly expands the programmable capabilities of trapped-ion architectures while maintaining low computational overhead and high potential for experimental implementation.

abstracts.value: Which pure states give uniform outcomes in several mutually unbiased measurements, and when can they form another measurement basis? We distinguish common unbiased states, their orthonormal completion, and further extension. For a displayed phase-deformed Fourier pair in dimension $2m$, a clock symmetry and skew antiunitary complete every prescribed common unbiased state to an explicit orthonormal basis. In dimension six, an amplitude-profile obstruction proves strong unextendibility of a given mutually unbiased triple when its original third-basis rays are invariant under the ternary clock. We give an exact nonproduct example and an application to a companion whose columns are localized at single Fourier frequencies. For every exact Hadamard matrix in a specified closed entrywise neighborhood of a fixed reference matrix, the coordinate and Hadamard bases have exactly 48 common unbiased rays but no third measurement basis, with a quantitative lower bound on the squared Gram defect of every six-column candidate. We also study auxiliary complex equations for common states, retaining algebraic multiplicities. For a flat unitary of order six with all $3\times3$ minors nonzero, the projective ray scheme is finite; each singular two-minor contributes two reduced isolated boundary points, and the affine coordinate algebra is finite-dimensional over $\mathbb{C}$. In every order, a critical-algebra identity preserves multiplicities; in dimension six it gives finiteness for a fixed phase fibre. Specialization over a discrete valuation ring controls complete reciprocal-orthogonal collections. A nonphysical Tao/Potts collection separates algebraic from physical solutions. These results do not determine the global maximum number of mutually unbiased bases or classify all triples.

titles.title: Mutually unbiased bases: common states, completion, and extension obstructions

abstracts.value: In this paper, we study the nature of wave packets and their decay behavior in the $κ$-Minkowski space. We employ techniques from singularity theory throughout our analysis. Specifically, we use methods from the theory of Lagrangian singularities and caustics to study the topology of the energy-level manifold. The Newton polyhedron method from the theory of oscillatory integrals is applied to analyze the decay behavior of wave packets. We find that for a generic Hamiltonian in the $κ$-Minkowski space, the associated wave packets exhibit different decay rates depending on the control parameter of the system. When the control parameter takes values on the cusp, the system exhibits decay of order $t^{-1/4}$; otherwise, it exhibits decay of order $t^{-1/2}$. This distinctive behavior of wave packets in the $κ$-Minkowski makes it fundamentally different from commutative spacetime.

abstracts.value: The entanglement structure of a bipartite pure state is characterized by its entanglement spectrum, or equivalently, by the family of Rényi-$k$ entanglement entropies with integer $k$. Taking the difference of two such entropies defines a quantity known as an entanglement spread, that is monotonous under local operations, and that vanishes if and only if the entanglement spectrum of the state is flat. We introduce a multipartite generalization of this notion which, for a fixed number $D\geq 3$ of parties, results in a collection of maps indexed by pairs of $D$-edge-colored graphs (obeying some condition). Each member of this collection takes the form of a difference of two multipartite Rényi entanglement entropies, each associated to a local unitary polynomial invariant (known in this context as a trace-invariant), and is shown to be monotonous under local operations. We then argue that a previously introduced family of so-called hypergraph-tensor (HT) states can be understood as a multipartite counterpart to the family of flat bipartite states. Indeed, we first prove that, when $D=3$, a tripartite pure state is HT if and only if it minimizes a particular (infinite) family of entanglement spreads. Second, we embed the set of HT states into the much larger family of spectral hypergraph-tensor (SHT) states, defined by a new Ansatz we introduce. We then prove that HT states can be uniquely characterized as the minimizers of some fixed entanglement spread among SHT states, for arbitrary $D\geq 3$. We also investigate SHT states in their own right: in particular, we characterize their orbits under local unitary transformations. Finally, along the way, the asymptotic large-$N$ expectation values of a number of entanglement spreads are computed in the Haar-random state of local dimension $N$.

titles.title: Multipartite entanglement spreads

abstracts.value: Full Pauli-basis tomography of an arbitrary $n$-qubit state uses the expectation values of all nonidentity Pauli observables. For multiqubit systems, prior knowledge that the state is pure allows some of these observables to be omitted while retaining uniqueness. We study two resulting notions of uniqueness: whether every pure state is uniquely determined among pure states (UDP), and whether every pure state is uniquely determined among all states, including mixed states (UDA). We derive quartic uniqueness certificates from the fourth elementary symmetric polynomial of operators in the real span of the omitted Pauli observables. An exact quartic identity shows that, for $n$-qubit systems with $n\geq 3$, every pure state is UDA whenever the omitted Pauli observables contain no four distinct operators that commute pairwise and multiply to $\pm I$. For three qubits, this condition is also necessary for UDP, yielding an exact characterization of both UDP and UDA. We further prove that UDP and UDA coincide for any number of qubits whenever the omitted Pauli observables commute pairwise. These results provide directly checkable structural criteria for certifying pure-state tomography from restricted Pauli measurements.

titles.title: Quartic Certificates for Pure-State Tomography with Pauli Measurements

abstracts.value: We present a generalization of T-duality, called $T_2$-duality, that captures certain aspects of U-duality in M-theory. In particular, it features backgrounds that contain a 2-gerbe over a principal torus bundle, structures familiar from eleven-dimensional supergravity backgrounds. In special cases, it also incorporates S-duality in a precise sense. Our main result is a theorem characterizing $T_2$-dual pairs through spans of categorified principal bundles with connections, giving explicit rules for constructing a $T_2$-dual for a given background. A number of explicit examples illustrate how the various characteristic classes are mapped between the left and right backgrounds. For two-dimensional torus fibers, we also relate our construction to the combination of dimensional reduction and T-duality that links eleven-dimensional supergravity to type IIB supergravity. Finally, we discuss how $T_2$-duality arises from a Buscher-like span of 3d sigma models.

abstracts.value: We construct a family of self-dual $(1+1)$-dimensional $\mathbb{CP}^1$ sigma models whose potentials $V$ are determined from pre-potentials $U$ by Platonic geometry. abstracts.value: Filamentation instabilities are generally regarded as detrimental to fast-electron transport in fusion plasmas because they increase beam divergence and redistribute deposited energy. Here, we use two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations coupled to a spin-dependent deuterium-tritium fusion module to investigate whether filamentation can instead transfer energy from counterstreaming electrons to prepolarized fusion ions. Over the parameter range examined, the calculated neutron yield increases with the saturated magnetic-field energy. The model further predicts anisotropic, spin-resolved neutron emission. The direction of maximum neutron polarization is approximately perpendicular to the dominant deuterium-tritium collision direction and evolves with the angular distribution of the reacting ions. These results suggest that beam filamentation can couple relativistic-electron energy to fusion ions and that polarized neutron emission may provide a reaction-weighted signature of the underlying plasma dynamics.
