2.6.1 Filling

The filling stage is the first stage in the experiment cycle during which UCNs are transported
from the anticipated UCN source at the FRM II into PENeLOPE’s storage volume. The
energy spectrum of the source plays a significant role, since PENeLOPE should be placed
at a height, where the maximum of the spectrum can be magnetically stored inside the
experiment, balanced by gravity. Guides that have VF > En are used to propagate UCNs
into the storage volume. The source and storage valves are open and the UCN switch directs
UCNs from the source to the storage volume. The UCNs are polarized after entering the
guide from the source before reaching the switch. A spin holding field, created by a current
flowing through the central rod, maintains UCN polarization once they enter into the storage
volume. The magnetic field created by the superconducting magnet to store UCNs is not on
at this time, so UCNs in the storage volume will interact with the inner and outer surface
walls of the storage volume.

2.6.2 Marginally Trapped UCN Cleaning

After the filling stage, the storage valve is closed and marginally trapped UCNs—those
with total energies exceeding the equipotential limit of ∼115 neV (only at nominal current)
imposed by the magneto-gravitational field—are removed. The UCN switch flap is then ro-
tated into the middle position to dump the remaining UCNs in the guides into the detector.
The absorber rings, placed at 700 mm above the bottom of the storage volume, remove
these UCNs leaving the UCNs in the storage volume with maximum total energies under
∼80 neV. The reason for setting the absorbers at that specific height will be explained in
section 2.6.3. The absorbers’ positions may be changed to cut off the energy spectrum at
other energies if needed. In the current configuration, the absorber is kept at a height of
∼700 mm above the bottom of the storage volume from the start of filling and continuing
until a certain cleaning time to sufficiently clean the MT UCN population.

27



2.6.3 Magnetic Field Ramp-up

At the beginning of the ramp-up stage, the UCN switch flap remains in its position to
open the path between the storage volume and the UCN detector. Since the storage valve
remains closed, the UCN detected at this point would be any that come from leaks through
the valves or background. A magnetic field is introduced by increasing the current through
the superconducting coils. The magnetic field increases over a span of 100 s until the nominal
current is reached. As the magnetic field strength increases, the total energy of UCNs is
altered due to the time-varying magnetic potential. This potential acts as a dynamic barrier,
effectively behaving as a moving mirror in the reference frame of the UCNs. Depending on
the phase of interaction, UCNs reflecting off this moving potential experience a change in
momentum, leading to either a gain or loss of kinetic energy. LFSs are heated or gain total
energy while the HFSs are cooled or lose total energy. By the end of this stage the LFSs
with total energies under 115 neV are completely trapped within the equipotential lines as
shown on the left side of Fig. 2.2. LFSs with higher total energies that are not completely
trapped within the equipotential lines are considered MT UCNs that still interact with
the material walls. The HFS population is attracted to regions close to the material walls
subjecting the HFS population to have more losses than the LFS population through wall
interactions.

2.6.4 High-field Seeker Cleaning

Once the magnetic field reaches its maximum value, the HFSs are removed via absorbers.
They are not trapped by the magneto-gravitational field within the storage volume at any
total energy. The absorber rings remove the HFSs by lowering down from their height of
∼700 mm to ∼5 mm above the bottom of the storage volume and are held there for roughly
20 s until they are brought back up to 700 mm. The storage valve is opened at the start of
this stage to release any marginally trapped UCNs or HFSs into the detector, serving both
to remove these unwanted UCNs and to provide a comparative measurement between runs.
The fully trapped LFSs are contained by the magnetic field and gravity so they should only
experience losses through β−decay during this stage even with the absorbers moving up
and down as long as it does not cross the 115 neV equipotential line. The proton detector
is activated during this stage to provide insight on how the population changes.

2.6.5 Storage

The storage stage starts after the HFS cleaning stage with a majority of fully trapped LFSs
plus a smaller fraction of the partially trapped MT UCNs and/or HFSs within the storage
volume. The absorbers stay at 700 mm, the magnetic field is held constant, the storage valve
stays open, and the UCN switch connects the storage volume to the UCN detector. The
proton detector is operational during the entirety of this stage to detect the decay protons

28



from UCN β−decay. For a full experiment cycle, the storage durations are t1 = 20 s and
t2 = 1550 s for this study, similar to the UCNτ experiment [13]. Systematic effects arise
from losses of marginally trapped UCNs and high-field seekers within the storage volume
during this stage.

2.6.6 Magnetic Field Ramp-down

After storage the remaining surviving UCN need to be counted in the UCN detector which
requires the magnetic field to be turned off. The UCN switch, storage valve, and absorber
remain in the same position as during the storage stage. The magnetic field is then decreased
slowly over 100 s until completely off. The detection of UCN starts during this stage. As the
magneto-gravitational equipotential barrier decreases, all UCNs, including those previously
trapped magnetically, are able to exit the storage volume and are guided to the UCN
detector.

2.6.7 Counting

Once the magnetic field is turned off, the remaining UCN within the storage volume are
given time to reach the detector. During this stage, the UCN switch, storage valve, and
absorber are in the same configuration as the previous stage. At this point, no distinction
between HFSs and LFSs is made since the detection is not spin sensitive. The final UCN
count is then acquired from the portion of UCN that were able to be detected. N1 and N2

from Eq. 1.10 are determined from the background corrected integral of UCN counts during
the ramp-down and counting stage for t1 and t2, respectively. The losses of UCN along the
way to the detector is modeled by a collection efficiency through simulations.

Three components at Technische Universität München (TUM) were available as viable can-
didates for PENeLOPE’s neutron transport between a UCN source, trap volume, and UCN
detector: a replica UCN guide, and two butterfly shutters. It was necessary to characterize
them to see if they were suitable for PENeLOPE’s τn measurement goal. We measured
the storage lifetime in the replica guide and the leak rates of the butterfly shutters. These

3.1 UCN Transport Components

UCN storage experiment cycles typically start with neutrons being transported from a
source to a storage volume. UCN transport components must be enclosed, such as cylindrical
guides with surface Fermi potential values large enough to allow UCNs to propagate while
reflecting off their inner surfaces. The enclosed volume must also have a suitable vacuum for
neutrons to have a low enough probability of being absorbed by rest gas. The reflectivity
of the guides plays a crucial role in the UCN transport efficiency, with surface roughness
being a key factor. Rough surfaces result in non-specular reflections, where neutrons scatter
in random directions rather than reflecting uniformly, causing a diffusive transport process.
This increases the number of reflections required for a neutron to travel a specific distance,
unlike smooth surfaces that enable specular reflection, thereby significantly reducing the
transmission efficiency of the guide. To address these challenges, extensive research and
development efforts are underway at various laboratories to enhance the properties of UCN
guides [26].

One method to achieve a guide with a smooth surface and high Fermi potential involves
replicating the glass-like smoothness onto nickel composites to fabricate replica guides. By

Replica guides, as shown in Fig. 3.1, have been shown to have good UCN transport charac-

thin-walled tube is not able to sustain a pressure difference of 1 bar so it is necessary to
enclose it within a stainless steel vacuum enclosure. The guides have a Fermi potential of
∼252 neV. Their surface roughness of under 10 Å[26] is equivalent to the roughness of the
original glass as it was copied from the sputtering. UCNs that propagate through the guide
still have a probability of being absorbed or upscattered with each wall interaction. During
the characterization experiment in Mainz, four 0.5 m replica guides were installed in series
to form a 2 m long storage volume.

3.2 Source Guide Characterization

3.2.1 TRIGA Reactor and UCN Source

The TRIGA reactor at Mainz offers two modes of operation, the first being a steady
state mode or continuous operation at 100 kW that provides a thermal neutron flux of
1012 n/(cm2 s). The other is a pulse mode which increases the instantaneous neutron flux
up to 250 MW within a 30 ms window 12 times per hour. The peak flux of neutrons is
up to 2 × 1015 n/cm2 s. The reactor core fuel elements have a chemical composition of
Uranium(20 % 235U)-Zirconiumhydride(UZrH) [28]. The hydrogen acts as a moderator,
providing inherent safety if the fuel elements increase in temperature. The neutrons pro-
duced during the heating will increase in energy, resulting in lower fission reaction rates until
fission is stopped completely. Figure 3.3 shows a horizontal cross-section of the reactor core
with beamports to guide neutrons out from the core. UCNs are produced at beamports C
and D. Beamport C was used for the PENeLOPE component characterization experiments.

32



Figure 3.3: Horizontal cut of the Mainz TRIGA reactor. Beamports A, B and D are centered
on the core while Beamport C was installed tangentially. Beamport C was used for the
PENeLOPE component characterization. Figure reproduced from [29].

Beamport C uses solid deuterium to convert thermal neutrons into ultracold neutrons.
Solid deuterium is an effective neutron moderator due to its low neutron absorption cross-
section and its ability to efficiently transfer energy through multiple elastic and inelastic
collisions within its lattice structure[30]. This process enables neutrons to lose energy and
transition into the ultracold regime. Figure 3.4 shows the schematic of beamport C. Thermal
neutrons incoming from the right of the diagram propagate through the stainless steel nose
of a neutron guide with an 80 mm inner diameter. The inner surface of the nose has the solid
D2-converter cooled down by liquid Helium to 5K covering the inner surface with an ap-
proximate thickness of 0.6 cm [28]. The supermirror neutron guides are made of glass coated
with thin layers of Nickel-Molybdenum (85/15) of increasing thicknesses from ∼10 nm to
∼150 nm alternating with several layers of Titanium (NiMo-Ti) of thicknesses increasing
from ∼9 nm to ∼20 nm. There are four neutron guides with 80 mm inner diameter. Two of
the guides have a length of 1250 mm, and the other two have a length of 300 mm. The VAT
shutter shown in Fig. 3.4 is installed between the two shorter 300 mm supermirror neutron
guides to open and close the beamline while the reactor is operational. An indirect neutron
flux reading was taken with a guide bend of 45 ◦ at end of beamport C and was measured
to be (4.8 ± 0.8) × 102 n/cm2 s consisting of UCNs and very cold neutrons (VCNs) [28].

3.2.4 UCN detector

The detector used in these experiments is a cascade UCN detector [31]. The cascade detector
is able to detect a UCN flux on the order of 107n/cm2s. It has an Al foil entrance window
with a Fermi potential of 54 neV and a thickness of 100 µm. Neutrons that pass through
the window interact with a 10B layer coated on a drift electrode leading to the reactions

10B + n −→ 7Li + α + 2.79 MeV (6%), (3.2)

and
10B + n −→ 7Li + α + 2.31 MeV (94%). (3.3)

The products from these reactions then ionize atoms in a gas mixture inside of the reaction
chamber, typically argon and carbon dioxide, ArCO2. The ionized atoms then interact with
gas electron multiplier (GEM) foils creating electrons. These electrons are then amplified
by being accelerating through an electric field in the holes between the GEM foils. The
amplified electrons then drift to a printed circuit board (PCB) readout. The PCB readout
is a key part of the electronic system, designed to capture, amplify, and transmit data about
neutron interactions occurring in the detector.

After filling, the storage period begins with both BS1 closing and BS2 remaining closed.
The duration of this period, tstore, varies between each run and there is a predefined sequence

Following the storage period, BS2 is opened to allow the surviving UCNs to exit the

such as systematic drifts in reactor power, that could affect the stored UCN counts. This
approach ensures that any fluctuations affect only specific subsets of UCN counts rather
than uniformly influencing all counts across multiple runs with a single storage time.

counting but the stored UCNs need time to propagate to the detector before only detecting

the BS1 leak are left within the apparatus reaching all the way to the detector. The last
stage of the experiment is a measurement of transmission counts with all shutters opened

3.2.6 Filling Time Optimization

The optimum filling time was found by measuring the saturation curve shown in Figure 3.13
of neutrons filled into the storage volume and then immediately emptied into the detector.
Neutron counts were recorded for various filling times {0 s, 4 s, 6 s, 8 s, 10 s, 20 s, 30 s,
40 s, 50 s}. Two or three runs were conducted for each of the filling times in an overall
randomized order of 23 runs and were plotted by averaging neutron counts obtained for
each predetermined filling time. The durations of the other stages were held constant for
each run: tstore = 10 s, tcounting = 80 s, and ttransmission = 50 s. tfill = 20 s was chosen as a
compromise between reaching saturation in the number of neutrons stored and saving time
as shorter filling durations allow more cycle runs in the same amount of time.

The BS1 and BS2 shutter leak experiments were conducted separately with the same set
up, once with BS1 and once with BS2. The leak rate measurements were obtained through
the four different configurations shown in Tbl. 3.2: 1. Both shutters were open for a trans-

measurement. 3. The leak measurement of VS was taken with VS closed and BS1/BS2
open. 4. Both shutters were closed for a background measurement. In all configurations, the

The experiment cycles for each configuration were done in increments up to a total duration

3.2.9 Storage Lifetime Experiment Analysis & Results

The storage lifetime is determined by filling neutrons into a trap, holding them for varying
storage times tstore and counting the surviving neutrons in a detector. The experiment was
conducted on two different days, designated Day 1 and Day 2.

Other measurements include background (BG) counts and BS1 UCN leak counts. BG
counts may come from different sources such as electronic BG that is always there, a cold
and faster neutron BG that come from when the reactor and UCN source are operational,
and a BG due to leaks through valves which is present when the reactor and UCN source are
operational but suppressed when more than 1 valve is closed. The cold and faster neutron
BG differs from the BG due to leaks through valves because cold neutrons do not have the

44



same property as UCNs of being totally reflected at any incident angle off a surface, so cold
and faster neutrons have a chance to interact with the guide surfaces but are not contained
like UCNs. The best period for background determination is the storage period, where both
shutters BS1 and BS2 were closed as seen in Fig. 3.10. The BG measured during the storage
period takes into consideration all the possible BGs that were mentioned above. These BG
measurements during storage are used to find an overall BG which includes a count from the
UCN leak through BS2 measured as well during the storage stage. The BS1 and BS2 leaks
affect the overall detected population. The BS1 leak during the storage period is illustrated
in Fig. 3.10. UCNs can propagate through a closed BS1 from both directions from the source
to the storage volume or from the storage volume to the source. The effect of UCNs leaving
the storage volume through BS leaks influences the measurement of τst. The incoming UCNs
from the source that leak into the storage volume provide a net positive effect since UCN
density will be higher upstream of BS1 compared to downstream (storage volume), so the
BS1 leak into the storage volume is constant since the source provides a constant flux. This
complicates the τst calculation through having a N(tstore) measurement that includes these
UCN gains and losses during storage.

originally planned comparison involving a separate 1 m replica guide was not possible due

results. This shows that the combination of the replica guides with the butterfly shutters
has higher UCN losses compared to the combination of the NiP coated guides with the
modified VAT valves [35] that were use at TRIUMF. The short storage lifetime may be
attributed to several factors: 1) gaps between the 0.5 m sections of the replica guides 2)
gaps in the butterfly valves when closed 3) losses in the bulk of the surfaces of the valves,
adapters and / or replica guides. It is hard to quantify 1 or 3, but a calculation can be made
to estimate 2. If the transmission of the closed valve is around 2 % of the open position, one
could define an effective opening of 2 % of its opening cross section that takes into account
all leak mechanisms such as the transmission through the bulk of the valve material. Taking
the geometry into account, one can then calculate the lifetime due to this effective opening.

Chapter Summary

This chapter focuses on analyzing three critical factors to determine whether the measure-
ment of the neutron lifetime using PENeLOPE can achieve the target precision of 0.1 s.
The following factors are examined:

1. Systematic Effects and Marginally Trapped (MT) UCN: Some UCNs are not
fully trappable within PENeLOPE, leading to systematic shifts in the measured neutron
lifetime. Of particular focus in this work is the contribution of marginally trapped (MT)
UCNs with total energies exceeding the magneto-gravitational trapping potential of 115 neV.
These neutrons may be lost during storage and cause shifts in the neutron lifetime mea-
surement. To address this issue, the duration of the MT cleaning stage, described in Section
2.6, is optimized to reduce the MT UCN population and minimize its impact on the mea-
surement.

2. Spin-Flip Probability of Stainless Steel: The walls of PENeLOPE’s storage volume
are composed of stainless steel, and UCN interactions with the storage walls can cause neu-
tron spin flips. This affects the ratio of low-field seekers to high-field seekers in PENeLOPE.
The spin-flip probability per wall bounce of stainless steel (βSS) is not well known. Only one
published result of βSS = 3.36 × 10−3 can be found and only in a conference presentation
that was not peer reviewed [24, 38]. This value is more than two orders of magnitude higher
than other β values for typical UCN component materials listed in Table 4.2. Due to the
potential uncertainty in this measurement, a parameter sweep of βSS with three values of
2 × 10−3, 10−4 and 10−5 was performed. A higher spin flip probability affects the viability
of PENeLOPE dramatically as will be shown in Section 4.3.3.

3. Number of Cycles Needed to Achieve a Statistical Precsion of 0.1 s: Section
4.3.4 presents the number of experimental cycles necessary to reach a statistical precision of

53



0.1 s on the neutron lifetime assuming PENeLOPE is operated at the planned UCN source
at the FRM II.

Methodology Employed

The method for analyzing the precision of the neutron lifetime measured using PENeLOPE
involves several steps. To start, simulations of UCNs in PENeLOPE are performed using
the PENTrack program, described in the next Section 4.1, to emulate full PENeLOPE
experiment cycles. Each of the seven stages of the experiment cycle, described in Section
2.6, are simulated independently. This is necessary since the stage durations need to be
varied to achieve an optimal compromise between statistical sensitivity and systematic
effects. To this end, the neutron population in PENeLOPE is divided up into 5 neV energy
bins and into low-field seekers (LFSs) and high-field seekers (HFSs). The assumption here
is that UCNs are characterized sufficiently by sorting them into a specific energy and spin
orientation bin. This is valid since the nature of diffuse wall reflections randomized neutron
trajectories efficiently so that the phase space of neutrons is in equilibrium. In practical
terms, this means that any neutron in a particular bin, no matter its location and velocity
vector has an almost equal probability of reaching any other accessible location in the
experiment. To properly connect one experimental stage to the next, a survival probability
is calculated for each energy bin which is used to evolve the energy distribution for LFSs and
HFSs through all seven stages. These distributions are created at each full second during
the whole experiment and all stage durations can be varied with this granularity without
requiring to run new simulations.

Furthermore, various combinations of stage durations can be chosen to make many ex-
periment cycles. This work focuses on varying one particular stage duration, the MT clean-
ing stage. All other stage durations are kept constant and set close to recommendations from
a previous publication [2]. Table 4.1 shows simulated stage durations that were arbitrarily
chosen and optimum durations that were chosen to simplify and reduce the optimization
routine to just varying the MT cleaning stage time.

To measure the exponential time constant of the neutron beta decay, two durations have
to be chosen for the magnetic storage period from Eq. 1.10. 20 s and 1550 s were adopted
following [13].

Simulation Stages and Key Analyses

UCN energy distribution histograms for both high-field seeking and low-field seeking neu-
trons from simulations were used to track UCNs through a PENeLOPE experiment cycle.
In the following, I provide a summary of the main objectives of each simulated stage as I
discuss them in Section 4.2.1 in further detail.
1. Filling Stage

• Objective: Normalize energy distributions of LFSs and HFSs based on the UCN
source flux at FRM II. The source fills neutrons into the storage volume of PENe-
LOPE. Pre-polarization is done between source and storage volume to reduce the
number of HFSs in PENeLOPE during filling.

• Stage is used to explain: LFS energy distributions are used to explain the nor-
malization process, which involves scaling the simulated production rate to the UCN
source flux using Equation 4.8. Although not shown, HFS distributions are normalized
through the same process.

2. Marginally Trapped (MT) Cleaning

• Objective: Remove UCNs from the storage volume that cannot be fully magnetically
stored, and which are prone to losses due to wall interactions.

• Stage is used to explain: The energy distributions of subsequent stages must be
connected to the filling stage, maintaining normalization relative to the UCN source, to
accurately track UCNs through the energy distributions across an entire PENeLOPE
cycle. As the spectrum progresses, it evolves due to effects introduced at each stage.

55



To account for this, the connection is established by calculating survival probability
distributions for each stage, which are then adjusted—both scaled and shaped—using
the experiment distribution from the preceding stage.

• Main Observations: Higher energy UCNs are effectively removed if the spin flip
probability of the storage walls is low enough.

3. Ramp-up Stage

• Objective: Turn on main magnetic field to transition from material storage in PENe-
LOPE to magnetic storage.

• Stage is used to explain: The LFS and HFS energy shift distributions are used to
observe the shifts caused by the magnetic field. Simulations that start with only LFSs
or only HFSs are created for all stages with a magnetic field to separate spin-flipped
UCN into additional energy distributions. This distinction ensures a comprehensive
understanding of how the magnetic field influences energy dynamics.

• Main Observations: High-field seekers lose energy, low-field seekers gain energy.

4. HFS Cleaning (Stages A & B)

• Objective: Remove HFSs via lowering of absorber rings.

• Stage is used to explain: HFS energy distributions are plotted to visualize the
removal of HFSs using absorber rings. Special attention is given to empty bins in
the energy distribution, as low statistics may lead to inaccuracies. Another approach
estimates the experimental distributions for these stages by utilizing calculated storage
lifetimes to determine the distributions.

Since the simulations with the magnetic field turned on start with either HFSs or
LFSs, this allows for observations on the impact of first-order spin flips to second-
order spin flips on the ratio of HFSs to LFSs stored in PENeLOPE. The production
of HFSs from spinflips is estimated for each simulation with different βSS.

5. Storage Stage

• Objective: To store LFSs with total energies under the magneto-gravitational po-
tential 115 neV for a short storage time of t1 = 20 s and a long storage time of
t2 = 1550 s.

• Stage is used to explain: The analysis focuses on the impact of marginally trapped
UCNs (MT UCNs) during this stage, evaluating how their losses during wall interac-
tions affect the neutron lifetime. However, the inclusion of β-decay in the simulations
introduces significant uncertainties, primarily due to low statistics. These uncertain-
ties could overshadow the effect of MT UCN losses on the neutron lifetime, making

56



it challenging to isolate and accurately assess their specific contribution. To get past
this issue, a filtering process is applied to exclude UCNs that undergo β−decay in the
simulations. This way, LFS energy distributions would only be dependent on other
loss mechanisms other than β−decay.

• Main Observations: UCN losses that occur during this stage contribute to a shift
of the measured neutron lifetime. Energy distributions are dependent on the value of
βSS . Low statistics in simulations makes β−decay have a high statistical uncertainty.

6. Ramp-Down and Counting Stage

• Objective: Magnetic field is turned off, LFSs and HFSs are counted.

• Stage is used to explain: The β−decay filtering applied in the storage stage is
corrected to account for the decay effects in the final combined energy distribution.
The ramp-down and counting stage’s energy distribution is connected with the storage
stage to obtain the final experiment distribution at the end of the PENeLOPE cycle.
The connection is done by applying the effect of this stage to the storage stage’s
experiment distribution. The collection efficiency is calculated for simulations with
each βSS .

4.1.2 PENTrack Inputs and Outputs

PENTrack has the option to accept computer-aided design (CAD) models in stereolitho-
graphic (STL) format to simplify the implementation of complex experiment geometries.
Each component of the CAD model is assigned material properties relevant for UCN inter-
action such as the scattering parameters, Fermi potentials VF and WF and the probability
of spin flip on wall bounce β. Material inputs for selected materials used in PENTrack
simulations for this study are shown in Table 4.2. Every component may be assigned user-
defined inactive times that allow them to appear or disappear at specified times during
the simulation. This is used to mimic moving parts, such as valves or switches, by copying
a component into different positions and changing their active times. Moving geometries
are not supported in PENTrack, yet. A simplified PENeLOPE CAD model used in these
simulations is shown in Figure 4.2.

59



The UCN switch has a flap inside that can be moved into three positions as described in
Section 2.4. To model this movement in PENTrack, because moving parts are not supported,
the flap is copied into the three positions and inactive times are assigned that would omit
these positions of the flap from the model at appropriate times. The storage valve is modeled
as a completely tight flat plate blocking the whole UCN entrance guide to PENeLOPE when
it is active. The absorber rings on the inside and outside walls of the PENeLOPE storage
volume, described in Section 2.3, are 10 cm high and protrude 5 mm into the storage volume
from the walls. Three possible positions are implemented depending on which absorber rings
are active or inactive.

Aside from material properties and changing inactive/active times of geometries used in
PENTrack, more user-defined inputs for UCN initial conditions such as maximum simulation
time, initial polarization, etc. are set up in a configuration file. Examples of these input
files are in Section A.1. Selected input parameters are seen in Table 4.3. In this research,
neutrons were the only particles simulated, while their decay products were excluded from
consideration. The simulated particles’ initial kinetic energy range along with an energy
spectrum function are also input parameters that are user-defined which may be utilized
to mimic a specific UCN source. In this work, the energy spectrum obtained from previous
simulations for the planned UCN source at FRM II is utilized [44]. The UCN source at FRM
II is described in Section 2.5. A magnetic field map may be used via table files created by
finite element software. A 2D, rotationally symmetric field map of the superconducting
magnet of PENeLOPE was created through the Opera3D software produced by Dassault
Systemes [45] in a previous study [37]. Additionally, a vertical current-carrying rod of 12.5 kV
in the center of PENeLOPE creates the spin holding field as described in Section 2.1. This
is represented by a line current in PENTrack and computed using the Biot-Savart law.

PENTrack records particle characteristics that are user-specified for the start and end
of a particle trajectory, such as initial and final simulation time t, Cartesian coordinates
(x, y, z), total energies H, and polarization p. They are saved in what will be referred to as
an end log file. This file can be saved as a ROOT [46] file which reorganizes the recorded
values into a data tree structure for analysis with ROOT or pyROOT. Other values that
may be recorded in the end log are: the number of times a particle hits a surface, Nhit, the
number of spin-flips per wall reflection, Nspinflip, and material number where the neutron
stopped being tracked, solidend.

PENTrack can also record the properties of the simulated particles at selected times
during the simulation in what are called snapshot log files. Similarly to the end log files,
the user inputs which properties are to be saved into the snapshot log files. The difference
between the snapshot and end log files is that the particle properties are recorded at user-
specified times during the simulation instead of at the end of a particle track. One can
use the snapshot logs to examine the neutron behavior throughout the simulation such as

4.1.3 Simulation Limitations

Before discussing the processes and effects in each stage of PENeLOPE’s experimental cycle
through simulations performed in this study, it is important to address the limitations in
statistics that became a bottleneck in the studies of PENeLOPE using simulations.

In PENTrack, only one particle is simulated at a time. The precision on the neutron
lifetime measurement using trap experiments depends heavily on the number of UCNs that
can be stored in the trap’s storage volume. From the results presented in Section 4.2.1, it
has been established that PENeLOPE is capable of storing approximately 107 UCNs in a
single run after filling from an operational UCN source at the FRM II. To reduce statistical
uncertainty, multiple runs must be performed to increase the total number of UCNs stored
and detected. The required number of runs was found to be 14 from the analysis in Section
4.3.4. This means that more than 108 UCNs would need to be simulated to achieve full
statistical precision.

When simulations of UCNs in PENeLOPE were first undertaken, the time required to
simulate full statistics was underestimated. To address the limitation of PENTrack simu-
lating only one particle at a time, the Cedar computing cluster from the Digital Research
Alliance of Canada [47] was utilized to execute PENTrack simulations on multiple CPUs in
parallel. By simulating each stage separately, it was found that the storage stage demanded
the most computational resources. This was due to the 2000 s duration of the storage simu-
lation, which is at least four times longer than other stages, and the magnetic field applied
during this stage. The magnetic field introduces additional computational complexity by
requiring more integration steps to process UCN trajectories along magnetic field lines,
thereby increasing the time per simulation.

Using PENTrack on Cedar [47], approximately 106 UCNs were simulated during the
storage stage by partitioning the workload into smaller tasks. Each PENTrack run was
configured to simulate 120 UCNs, and 10 jobs were submitted simultaneously. Each job
consisted of 1000 tasks, with each task running on a single CPU, allowing 1000 CPUs to be
used concurrently. This configuration enabled the simulation of 120,000 UCNs per job. By
repeating this process across multiple jobs, 106 UCNs were achieved, but this was still several
orders of magnitude below the required statistics. Simulating these 106 UCNs consumed
roughly 75,000 CPU hours. Extrapolating to full statistics would require approximately
7.5 × 106 CPU hours, or about 313 days on Cedar.

Achieving full statistics was further complicated by the intent to simulate different mate-
rial properties, such as varying the spin-flip probability βSS of stainless steel on PENeLOPEs
storage surfaces. Each βSS value increased the total simulation time by a factor of three due
to the need to simulate multiple configurations of PENeLOPE.

62



Given the unrealistic timeframe required to achieve full statistics, the analysis was com-
pleted by rescaling results from the lower-statistics simulations, accounting for the higher
statistical uncertainties that arise from this approach.

4.2 Simulating a PENeLOPE Cycle using PENTrack

PENTrack has the ability to simulate a full PENeLOPE run cycle in one simulation by
changing the input parameters to follow each of the seven stage configurations. Attempting
to simulate a full PENeLOPE run for each combination of stage durations would be ex-
ceedingly computationally costly in both time and storage. To avoid this bottleneck, each
stage in the PENeLOPE cycle is simulated separately. These stage simulations are then
connected to complete a run cycle through probability distribution histograms of UCN en-
ergy which are recorded each second during each stage. This process is described in more
detail in Sections 4.2.2 and 4.2.3.

The analysis is performed by storing the UCN population within PENeLOPE’s storage
volume into histograms of UCN total energy H using 5 neV bins between −200 and 300 neV
as seen in Figure 4.4. The initial and final total energies Hstart and Hend are defined to be the
sum of the kinetic and potential energies without the rest mass energy of the UCNs. Both,
high-field seekers and low-field seekers are recorded. Figures of LFS energy distributions
from simulations with βSS = 2 × 10−3 are used to describe UCNs in the filling and MT
cleaning stage simulations.

4.2.1 Filling Simulation

Simulations of the filling stage begin with UCNs being produced on a disk surface inside
a polished steel guide connected to the storage volume, as seen in Fig. 4.2. This mimics
an incoming UCN flux from an active source. PENeLOPE was planned to be installed
at FRM II which is currently not in operation. Therefore, simulations were conducted in
previous studies to determine the energy spectrum shape of UCNs detected immediately
after the UCN source at FRM II [2]. This energy spectrum shape is modeled as a polynomial
function only valid for UCNs with kinetic energies between 100 to 300 neV as FRM II has
a deuterium source that boosts UCN by ∼100 neV. The disk source produces UCN at its
surface with a cos(θ) angular distribution. The production rate of UCNs in the simulation
Ṅprodsim is ∼ 20000 neutrons per second for a total filling time tfill of 499 s. The energy
distribution is shown in Figure 4.3. With respect to the kinetic energy spectrum mentioned
above, the total energy is shifted downward by ∼ 103 neV, resulting in an energy range of
[-5 neV, 200 neV]: the reference point and coordinate origin of the simulation is placed at
the bottom of the PENeLOPE storage volume, approximately 1.01 m above the neutrons’
starting points. Also notice that the shift is not precisely -103 neV since the disk source
has some vertical extent, altering the shift a bit. UCNs with an initial energy Hstart greater

ignored since they either do not make it in or they end up absorbed or upscattered shortly

4.2.2 Marginally Trapped Cleaning Simulation

MT Cleaning stage simulations should begin as a continuation of the filling stage, with
UCNs trapped in the storage volume. To start a simulation with neutrons inside of a volume
instead of a source surface in PENTrack, a source volume geometry is needed. The chosen
geometry for the source volume is nearly identical to the PENeLOPE storage volume with
the exception of a decrease in size of 10 mm inward from all storage surfaces. This reduction
in volume accounts for the absorber geometries placed at the surface walls, preventing
UCNs from being created in the space where the absorbers would be. The source volume
also includes a portion of the guide volume above the storage valve. The lower end of this
additional guide volume is positioned 400 mm below the storage bottom, centered 725 mm
horizontally from the storage center, and offset 5 mm inward relative to the guide surface.
The source volume is not directly shown but is defined as occupying the space within the
storage volume and the guide volume above the storage valve, as illustrated in Fig. 4.2. The
decision to include this guide in the source volume was based on the observation that UCNs
occupy this space after filling and are stored once the storage valve is closed. Studies on
UCNs within this guide volume are beyond the scope of this work and will be investigated
in the future.

Phase Space Weighting

A UCN population within a material trap can be modeled as a classical gas capable of
achieving a quasi-statistical equilibrium known as mechanical equilibrium. UCN popula-
tions in mechanical equilibrium are characterized by isotropy of the gas in momentum
space [19]. Since UCNs have a chance to reflect off of material walls in a non-specular fash-
ion, the momentum vectors of stored UCNs will be uniformly distributed in all directions
after many wall bounces. The momentum phase space available for a given UCN density
is energy dependent, so gravity, magnetic fields, and Fermi potentials change the accessible
phase space of the UCN gas. For example, if the UCN gas is in a gravitational field, the

67



available phase space contracts with height. To simulate neutrons starting within PENe-
LOPE’s storage volume, the available phase space must be considered to determine their
initial positions, ensuring a more realistic simulation. In PENTrack, implementing phase
space weighting requires specifying a source volume geometry. This geometry defines the
region where neutrons originate and serves as the basis for initializing the phase space
weighting process.

PENTrack simulates a neutron by first choosing a random initial position within the
source volume geometry, with an initial kinetic energy sampled from a predefined distribu-
tion. When phase space weighting is active, a minimum potential energy Vmin of the system
is found by randomly selecting many spatial points inside the volume and overwriting Vmin

if Vnew < Vmin. Rejection sampling is then done by sampling particles with various starting
times and positions which are only simulated through being accepted by a probability of

p =

Connecting Stage Simulations

As mentioned in the introduction of this chapter, UCNs are simulated in separated PENe-
LOPE cycle stages. The UCN energy distributions of each stage then are independent from
one another and need to be connected to add dependency to show how the UCN energy
spectrum evolves from the beginning to end of a given PENeLOPE cycle. Simulations of
UCNs stages after the filling stage start with flat (or arbitrary) UCN energy distributions
because the effects being simulated are not dependent on other stages. UCNs are tracked
through a stage before adding dependency from previous stages. The connection between
the energy distributions of a given stage with the previous stage in a PENeLOPE cycle is
established by multiplying the survival probability histogram of a given stage by the output
energy distribution of the previous stage at a chosen stage duration.

UCN Energy Spectrum Cut by Absorber

As described in Chapter 2, an absorber is used to clean the UCN energy spectrum before
the magnetic field is turned on. Two polyethylene absorber rings with heights of 100 mm
are placed 685 mm above the bottom of the storage volume, seen in Fig. 4.2 as the upmost
absorbers, one on the inside wall of the storage volume and one on the outside wall. UCN
above 80 neV can reach these rings and have therefore a high probability of being removed
from the spectrum. This cutoff is chosen, rather than the magneto-gravitational trapping
potential of 115 neV, to compensate for UCN heating/cooling introduced by an increasing
magnetic field during the ramp-up stage (see Section 4.2.3). The chosen cutoff of 80 neV
guarantees that most of the LFS population is fully trapped by the magnetic field after
heating determined in previous absorber studies [37].

4.2.3 Ramp-up Simulation

In PENeLOPE, a magnetic field is used to create a magnetic trapping potential that confines
low-field seekers within the storage volume, preventing them from colliding with the walls.
The field is created by a current running through superconducting coils. During the ramp-up
stage, current is gradually increased through the coils over 100 s as they can only be ramped
so fast, which produces a magnetic field. The field is implemented in PENTrack using a 2D

73



axisymmetric field table. Interpolation is used in between the data points. PENtrack allows
a scaling of this field that we use to mimic a ramping coil by changing the scaling factor
linearly from 0 to 1 in 100 s.

The magnetic trapping potential reduces the accessible phase space volume. Applying
Liouville’s theorem, which states that the phase-space density remains constant as the
system evolves with time, UCNs in the storage volume gain absolute momentum or energy
as a result of the applied magnetic field. Figure 4.10 shows the energy shift produced by the
reduction in phase space after applying the magnetic field during the ramp-up simulation
of either the LFS or HFS populations. The average heating of the LFSs is ∆H ≈ 22.28 ±
4.14 neV while the HFSs cool by ∆H = −94.03 ± 31.04 neV.

UCNs also suffer energy changes when they spin-flip due to wall reflections. For example,
when a low-field seeker with a total energy of 130 neV and a gravitational potential of 15 neV
hits the wall where the magnetic field is 1.66 T, corresponding to Vm = 100 neV, it only
has a kinetic energy of 15 neV. If the spin flips upon wall interaction, Vm changes sign and
the total energy is now -85 neV, but the kinetic energy does not change. This, however has
the effect, that the neutron cannot reach any point in space where the magnetic field is
less than 1.4 T. It cannot reach most of the storage volume of PENeLOPE anymore and
is bound to the high-field region close to the walls. Therefore, this now high-field seeking
neutron undergoes many wall interactions until it is either absorbed or upscattered.

The energy distributions of stored LFSs and HFSs, respectively, after a ramp-up time of
tRamp-up = 100 s, are shown in Fig. 4.11. A comparison of the distributions from the end of
the MT cleaning stage (Fig. 4.9) to the end of the ramp-up stage (Fig. 4.11) clearly reveals
LFS and HFS energy shifts. The magnetic field increases the total energy of the LFSs and
decreases the total energy of the HFSs. Subsequently, only HFSs and MT LFSs undergo
wall reflections and are prone to losses and wall-spin flips. Low field seekers below 115 neV
are stored purely by gravity and the magnetic field, and they don’t interact with the walls
anymore.

Separating Simulations with a Magnetic Field

Due to computational limitations that increase statistical uncertainty (discussed in Section
4.1.3), it was of interest to separate the simulations by simulating only HFSs or LFSs when
the magnetic field was turned on. This approach aimed to increase the number of HFSs
simulated, as HFS simulations required less time to complete compared to LFS simulations
by a factor of 3 in CPU hrs for simulating 106 UCNs.

The primary motivation for this separation approach is to ensure that the simulations
portray the loss of HFSs, and also energy shifts due to spin flips, as realistically as possible
in the stages that have the magnetic field turned on. If these processes are inaccurately
scaled, they could lead to misleading results. For example, if one HFS simulation is scaled
to represent 1000 actual HFSs through normalization to the UCN source, its loss in the

74



simulation would translate to the simultaneous loss of 1000 neutrons from the same effect,
which could distort the interpretation of the simulation outcomes.

LFSs tend to survive longer because all simulated LFSs with energies below 115 neV
remain trapped without colliding with the walls, leading to longer simulation durations. In
contrast, HFSs have a higher chance of colliding with the walls, resulting in their removal or
loss and consequently shorter simulation times. By increasing the number of HFSs simulated,
the statistical uncertainty specifically associated with HFS simulations could be reduced.

Simulations with a magnetic field were divided into two categories and used to study
the starting populations separately: those beginning with only LFSs (referred to as LFS
simulations) and those starting with only HFSs (referred to as HFS simulations). UCNs
that spin-flip in these LFS and HFS simulations are treated separately. Analyzing UCN spin
flips from separate simulations proved to be challenging, as discussed in detail in Section
4.2.4. With simulations already done and an analysis script that takes this treatment into
account, it was not a priority to redo the simulations or scripts for this work. To address this
issue in future PENeLOPE simulation studies, it is recommended that the simulated LFSs
and HFSs begin as a complete UCN population to mitigate this difficulty. Although this
difficulty persists, connecting the UCN energy distributions from the stages of simulations
with the magnetic field turned on with other previous UCN energy distributions was still
achievable and is discussed below.

4.2.4 HFS Cleaning Simulation

High-field seekers that survive the ramp-up stage, or those produced by spin flips after the
ramp-up stage, are attracted to the storage walls, increasing their wall reflection rate as the
available space for them decreases. This is seen in a spatial plot of HFSs and magnetically
trapped LFSs within PENeLOPE’s storage volume in Figure 2.3. The magnetically trapped
LFSs stay within the low field region while the HFSs collect near the storage walls due to
the high magnetic field regions attracting them there. The MT LFSs are not displayed as
they can be present anywhere in the storage volume. The HFSs and MT LFSs must then
be cleaned out of the storage volume to minimize UCN loss during the magnetic storage
period. The stage after ramp-up is called the HFS cleaning stage because the absorbers
move down along the storage walls, cleaning HFSs and MT LFSs while avoiding interaction
with fully trapped LFSs.

The absorber starts from its initial height of 685 mm and ends at 5 mm relative to
the bottom of the storage volume. Previous work indicates that the total HFS cleaning
procedure takes 60 s to reduce the ratio of HFSs to MT LFSs to 10−4. This result is based
on simulations in which neutrons fill the storage volume from a source without a polarizer
installed in the source guide and assumes a spin-flip probability of βSS = 10−5 for the
storage walls [2]. These 60 s were split between lowering the absorbers 20 s to move to the
bottom of the storage volume, holding them there for 20 s, then back up to their original

79



position over the last 20 s. To simulate the movement of the absorbers, four absorber ring
geometries are included in the PENeLOPE CAD model: two are placed near the storage
walls in a half-way position at 340 mm above the storage volume bottom to compensate
for lowering the absorbers and two are placed at the bottom position at 5 mm above the
storage bottom for when the absorbers are moved to their lowest position. This is done
because moving geometries are not supported in PENTrack yet.

The HFS cleaning stage is then split into two separate simulations that either have the
absorber in the middle position (HFS cleaning (A) stage) or the bottom position (HFS
cleaning (B) stage). This separation allows for the characterization of the absorbers’ ef-
fectiveness at cleaning HFSs while in each position. Both HFS cleaning stages have total
simulation times of 100 s as listed in Tbl. 4.1. In this study, both HFS cleaning stage (A)
and (B) durations were set to 20 s, assuming that nearly all HFSs are cleaned before the
absorber moves back up, disregarding the additional 20 s needed for the absorbers to return
to their initial height.

For the next study in this stage, only the HFS energy distribution from HFS simulations
is determined. The limitation of analyzing this population will be explored at the end of
this section.

High-Field Seeker Cleaning Stage (A): Absorber in the Middle Position

High-field seekers are removed at a high rate when the absorber is in the middle position.
Figure 4.14 shows the simulated input and output distributions of the HFS cleaning stage
(A) as green and red bins respectively. The number of HFSs in the green bins must be large
enough to give as small a statistical uncertainty as possible on the effect of the cleaning.

If the simulated output distribution has empty bins, then there is uncertainty that would
be corrected by increasing the number of HFSs that are simulated for this stage. A statistical
problem arises of how to treat these resulting ’empty’ bins if simulating more HFSs is not
possible. A different method is used to determine the HFS counts as a function of Hstart at
the end this stage that avoids this pitfall.

UCN Spin-flips During the High-field Seeker Cleaning Stage (A)

The spin-flip effect, which may occur when ultracold neutrons (UCNs) collide with the
storage walls, presents challenges for the current methods of simulation data analysis used
in this study. These are:

1. Simulations of stages with a magnetic field begin with either LFSs or HFSs exclusively.
The reason for separating these simulations is discussed in Section 4.2.3. Spin-flipped
LFSs or HFSs are not combined with the rest of their population at this point for these
distinct simulations, but they are combined in order to connect with other stages.

2. The HFS counts vs. HFS cleaning stage time plots, such as the one in Fig. 4.15,
account for HFSs that have undergone spin-flips in the HFS simulations, where they
spin-flip an even number of times and remain HFSs. These spin-flipped HFSs occur
randomly during the stage which affects the storage lifetime fit. Currently, these plots
do not include HFSs that are produced by an odd number of spin flips from the LFS
simulation.

3. The HFS counts from the LFS simulations have to be analyzed separately as they
are not considered in the HFS counts vs HFS cleaning (A) stage time plots for each

85



Hstart bin. The importance of these HFSs was underestimated initially and would have
required a complete rewrite of the analysis script.

For the first challenge, the spin-flipped populations can either be kept in separate distri-
butions to characterize their specific loss rate or they are combined with the HFS simulation
total energy distributions. Spin-flip populations were kept separated to try to study the im-
pact of first order spin-flips on the number of HFSs and LFSs.

For the second challenge, HFSs that spin-flip back into HFSs (2nd order spin flips)
can impact the HFS counts vs HFS cleaning (A) stage time plots due to fluctuations in
HFS counts over time. Binning HFSs by Hstart keeps these spin-flipped HFSs in the same
energy bin as they re-appear in the distribution at random times within the stage. If HFSs
were binned with respect to Hend, the fits of those plots would yield inaccurate lifetimes
as the fits would try find a solution that incorporates the production of HFSs through
an exponential term. The storage lifetime τ(HFS Cleaning A)(Hstart) values from fits are then
average approximations, when using Hstart bins, that include the fluctuation in bin counts
produced by higher-order spin-flips that turn HFSs back into HFSs after depolarization
from wall interactions multiple times. A 25 s duration is used to record HFS counts in order
to determine storage lifetimes through fits, instead of the full 100 s stage duration. In the
plots that consider the full 100 s, empty bins can be sporadically repopulated by doubly
spin-flipped HFSs, which may distort the calculated τ(HFS Cleaning A)(Hstart) values.

For the third challenge, the ratio of the number of HFSs from LFS simulation spin
flips over the total number of LFSs that survive until the end of the stage Rsurviving HFS is
estimated to measure the ratio of HFSs to LFSs that remain in the storage volume at the
end of the HFS cleaning (A) stage. This estimation is done by finding the total amount of
HFSs produced through LFS spin flips and decaying this by an associated storage lifetime
to find the ratio of surviving HFS.

Rsurviving HFS is estimated for all three βSS. The number of LFSs converting to HFSs over
100 s is denoted as N∗

4.2.5 Storage Simulation

The UCN population that is carried through the cycle to reach the storage stage is dependent
on the duration of all prior stages. The cleaning stages were introduced to reduce the
marginally trapped LFSs and the HFSs before storage because they both contribute to a
systematic shift on the neutron lifetime. The goal of the systematic effect study in this
thesis is to calculate the shift of the neutron lifetime that is caused by the loss of marginally
trapped UCNs (MT UCNs)—low-field seekers that have total energies above the magneto-
gravitational trapping potential—through wall interactions during this stage between the
short and long storage times of tstorage = 20 s and tstorage = 1550 s.

Recalling Eq. 1.11, there are several neutron loss channels that impact the effective
neutron lifetime measurement. The contribution of these loss channels to the lifetime can
be expressed as

the contribution from MT UCNs being lost during storage through wall interactions, this

the MT UCNs and HFS populations allows for individual evaluation of their systematic
shift contributions to the measured neutron lifetime. More loss channels may be present
that are not mentioned because they are out of the scope of this study. The terms fNLFS

and fNHFS represent subpopulations of the total UCN population that experience losses
during the experiment cycles, with their respective loss rates characterized by lifetimes τMT

and τHFS. From Equation 4.11, τMT will be measured in order to calculate the systematic

study the loss mechanism of MT UCN lost through absorption or upscattering upon wall

of τMT without interference from the inherent randomness of the decay process. Once this
loss mechanism is fully understood, β−decay can be reintroduced to assess its additional
impact. If it isn’t removed then a reduction of the statistical uncertainty must occur to
make it be below 0.1 s. This is done by simulating even more neutrons than required for a

4.2.6 Ramp-down and Counting Stage Simulation

The ramp-down and counting stages are simulated together because high energy UCN can
reach the detector already during the ramp-down of the magnet. At the beginning of the
ramp-down stage, LFSs shift to lower energies and HFSs shift to higher energies as more
phase space becomes accessible with the decreasing magnetic field.

The magnetic storage potential Vtrap decreases to 0 neV over 100 s. However, since the
absorbers remain at their initial height in the storage volume, a cut off potential at 80 neV
is still present, cleaning out a portion of UCNs during this stage. The MT LFSs are the
first to leave the storage volume through the feeder into the UCN transport system, where
they have a chance to reach the detector downstream. HFSs are produced by MT LFSs
that undergo spin flips at the walls. These HFSs are lost more quickly than MT LFSs
before the magnetic field is fully ramped down. After ramp-down, the magnetically stored
LFSs, marginally trapped LFSs and HFSs, are treated as one population as all of them
have similar losses through wall reflections. Only a fraction of the total initial population
of UCNs, quantified later in a detection efficiency calculation, reaches the UCN detector,
however more losses occur at the entrance window of the detector as UCNs also have to pass
through an aluminum foil to be counted. For the purposes of the PENeLOPE simulations,
the UCN detector is assumed to have a detection efficiency of 100%.

Figure 4.23 shows the stored UCN energy distribution (blue) at the start of the stage and
the detected UCN energy distribution (red) at tRD Counting = 499 s for the βSS = 2 × 10−3

simulations. A shift to lower energies from the blue to the red distributions shows the
increase in accessible phase space. The final population distribution is only a fraction of the
stage’s starting population. The collection efficiency ηcol is calculated as

ηcol = Total UCN Detected
Population at the End of Storage (4.12)

where each population is obtained through summed counts of UCN from the experiment
energy distributions. Table 4.6 lists the results of ηcol for each βSS simulation. The two
storage durations, tstorage = 20 s and tstorage = 1550 s, were studied to see if a deviation is
seen between the collection efficiencies from different experiment runs. It is important to
note that a correction was applied to the filtered storage stage experimental distributions to
reintroduce β-decay and account for the UCNs that would have decayed during the storage
stage. This corrected storage stage experiment distribution was then used to determine the
experiment distribution of the ramp-down or counting stages.

Figure 4.24 shows a plot of the detection efficiencies vs βSS. The detection efficiencies of
run cycles with 20 s storage durations are the blue dots, while the UCN detection efficiencies
from 1550 s storage duration cycles are the orange dots. The difference between the detection
efficiencies of the short and long storage durations shows that there are some surviving MT
UCNs that are lost between the short and long storage times. The difference between them

94



gets smaller as βSS decreases as not many MT UCNs are within the storage volume compared
to the amount that would be in the storage volume with larger βSS values. The detection
efficiency also saturates with lower βSS. One reason this occurs is because with a lower spin-
flip probability, fewer HFSs are produced through LFS spin flips, and with the magnetic
field still active but being reduced, the HFSs would interact with the storage walls more
frequently than marginally trapped LFSs.

The discrepancy in the detection efficiencies for the two higher βSS generates a sys-
tematic shift on the neutron lifetime measurement. This demonstrates that higher spin flip
probabilities at the wall are problematic for PENeLOPE. The systematic shifts from the
discrepancies are listed in Tbl. 4.6. The resulting shift for βSS = 10−5 meets the precision
goal of 0.1 s because the energy distributions did not change drastically from 20 s to 1550 s
of storage. This already shows how important the value of βSS is in order to continue de-
veloping PENeLOPE. βSS would have to be verified and possibly corrected for before using
PENeLOPE for neutron lifetime experiments.

4.3 PENeLOPE Simulation Analysis & Results

4.3.1 Polarization Ratio within a PENeLOPE Cycle

The PENeLOPE simulations generated for this study provide detailed information on the
LFS, HFS, and MT LFS populations at every second throughout the cycle. HFSs and
MT LFSs will never be fully trapped as they always have a chance to be absorbed or
upscattered through wall collisions. It is important to analyze these two populations through
an experiment cycle as they are undesired and need to be kept at a minimum in order to
achieve the precision goal of measuring the neutron lifetime with an uncertainty of 0.1 s.

The changes in the number of LFSs and HFSs within PENeLOPE’s storage volume are
examined for an experiment cycle by calculating the polarization p defined in Eq. 2.2.

p is calculated at any given point of the experiment cycle, with a granularity of one
second, by finding the number of LFSs and HFSs at that given time. To study how p changes
throughout an experiment cycle, one specific PENeLOPE experiment run is chosen. The
selected run cycle has the MT cleaning stage duration set to tMT cleaning = 199 s and the
storage stage duration set to tstorage = 1550 s while the other stage durations follow the
chosen simulation stage times in Tbl. 4.1. The polarization distributions are seen in Figure
4.25. The simulations with different βSS =

{
2 × 10−3, 10−4, 10−5} have p values per second

colored blue, orange, and green respectively. Only the LFS and HFS populations within
the storage volume are used in the p calculations. However, p for the UCNs that reach the
detector after the storage stage are also shown in red, purple, and brown markers.

The following describes the polarization trend and effects on UCNs that influence po-
larization during each stage in a PENeLOPE run cycle:

1. Filling: The polarizer and spin flipper produce a maximum polarization of 94 %
downstream from the UCN source, maximizing the stored LFS population. As LFSs
propagate through the guides to the storage volume and also in the storage volume
itself, they collide with the guide surfaces and storage surfaces, which may cause them
to spin-flip into HFSs, leading to a decrease in polarization. These spin flips would
occur mostly in the storage volume as this is where UCNs experience more frequent
interactions with the walls. When the UCN source is active, it introduces new UCNs,
mostly LFSs, into the system, which should increase polarization. Polarization should
also rise as stored HFSs spin-flip back into LFSs.

Despite these effects, a general decreasing trend in polarization is seen in all three
experiment runs with different values of βSS. The significance of a higher βSS is evident
in the run with βSS = 2 × 10−3 shown in blue. This indicates that a higher spin-flip
probability per wall bounce causes polarization p to decrease more rapidly to its
equilibrium value (which is not fully reached within the chosen filling time, but still
remains p > 0 after 199 seconds).

flipped.

6. Ramp-down and Counting: UCN counting begins after storage once UCNs are able
to leave the storage volume and reach the detector. Polarization of UCNs residing in
the storage volume during the ramp-down stage shows how the populations evolve. In

the decrease in polarization as the magnetic field ramps-down and eventually turns
off. During ramp-down, the magnetically trapped LFSs slowly start hitting the walls.
Eventually, the magnetic trap disappears and all LFSs hit the walls, where they can
either be lost through wall interactions, lost through β−decay, spin-flipped into HFSs,
or later detected. The decrease in LFSs and the increase in HFSs from spin flips at
the walls leads to a lower polarization of UCNs in the storage volume.

Although p is not a significant value for UCN remaining in the storage volume after
ramp-down, as the entire UCN population is counted at the end of a run cycle, the
polarization of the detected UCN during the counting stage can provide insights into
the collection efficiency ηcol from Eq. 4.12. The detection of UCN is done continually,
hence an average polarization is taken that calculates a polarization at a given time
based on the integration of all HFS and LFS counts that have been detected up to
that point. This average polarization will be defined as a cumulative polarization
The detected polarization is calculated from all UCN detected since the start of the
ramp-down stage.

Spin flips on wall reflections reduce the cumulative polarization of the neutron ensem-
ble in PENeLOPE. So the UCNs detected over time become less and less polarized,

100



but since the cumulative p includes all LFSs and HFSs detected, the polarization of
the detected UCNs stays above the instantaneous polarization of LFSs and HFSs in
PENeLOPE’s storage volume. This polarization is illustrated in Fig. 4.25 shown by
the red, purple, and brown markers representing polarization from the run cycles with
βSS =

{
2 × 10−3, 1 × 10−4, 1 × 10−5}, respectively.

The polarization also saturates around different points in each run with the different
βSS values. No matter how small the ratio of polarized UCNs is at later times in
the stages, there are fewer HFSs and LFSs which would not change the detected
polarization by a significant amount. Hence this cannot decrease the detected p values
down anymore, therefore it stabilizes at a certain value.

The polarization trends are, overall, inversely correlated to βSS as the lowest p values
are seen in the runs with highest βSS of 2 × 10−3. With higher polarization, there are more
HFSs in the storage volume during storage and if they are lost through wall interactions
they introduce a systematic effect that shifts the neutron lifetime. The shift of the neutron
lifetime from this effect is outside of the scope of this thesis.

4.3.2 Marginally Trapped LFS Population within a PENeLOPE Cycle

Marginally trapped low-field seeker neutrons (MT LFS), also known as MT UCNs through-
out this thesis, are UCNs that have total energies above the magneto-gravitational trapping
potential of 115 neV. It is of significant interest to track MT UCNs throughout an experiment
cycle because they are the focus of this precision study on the neutron lifetime measurement
using PENeLOPE. If they are lost during storage through wall interactions they cause a
systematic shift of the neutron lifetime measurement discussed in Section 4.2.5. The MT
LFS population is characterized by the ratio

RMT = MT LFS Population
Total LFS Population . (4.13)

Similarly to the p trend, RMT is plotted for the same run cycles used in the polarization
ratio analysis in section 4.3.1, as shown in Figures 4.27 and 4.28. The same marker col-
ors representing as in the polarization plots for each βSS are chosen for theses figures. In
a PENeLOPE experiment cycle, the LFS population is divided by a trapping potential
threshold into magnetically trapped and marginally trapped LFSs. The total trapping en-
ergy threshold of 80 neV, set by the absorber rings before the ramp-up stage, compensates
for the energy shift caused by the magnetic field, which is activated later in the ramp-up
stage. This shift increases the total energy of LFSs by approximately 35 neV, as shown
in Fig. 4.10. LFSs exceeding this energy threshold are classified as marginally trapped in
the experiment cycle when the magnetic field is turned off. When the magnetic field is ac-

101



tive, the trapping energy threshold rises to 115 neV, so LFSs above this new threshold are
considered marginally trapped.

1. Filling: Incoming MT LFSs from the spin flipper enter the storage volume at a higher
rate before the slower UCNs reach the storage volume, but this isn’t a significant effect
that would change RMT by much after a few seconds into the stage. The MT LFS
population decreases primarily due to the absorbers positioned at a height of 700 mm,
which remove MT LFSs (>80 neV), while also cleaning out some magnetically stored
LFSs above 70 neV for an added safety margin. MT LFSs are also considered lost if
they spin-flip into HFSs on wall reflections.

2. MT Cleaning: Since no additional UCNs are produced after the filling stage, a
decrease in RMT is apparent as the MT LFSs are cleaned by absorbers and lost through
wall reflections. The MT LFS population rapidly declines, with RMT values dropping
to below approximately 1 % in Fig. 4.28. Following this initial decrease, the loss
rate is smaller because the generation of MT LFSs from spin-flipped HFSs becomes
more pronounced in the reduced MT LFS population. By the end of the cleaning
stage, RMT decreases further to below 0.01%. The absorbers effectively eliminate MT
LFSs resulting in a storable LFS population exceeding 99.99 % after 199 s seconds
when considering only the number of LFS within the storage volume because RMT

ignores the number of HFSs. This statistical loss process can be modeled by one or
more exponential decay function(s) because the rate of absorption is proportional to
the number of neutrons leading to exponential behavior. The decreasing MT LFS
population trend is shown in Fig. 4.28 as an initially steep downward trend that
gradually flattens, the slope becoming less negative over time.

3. Ramp-up: The magnetic field increases during ramp-up causing LFSs to gain ∼35 neV.
This increase is due to the reduced phase space volume available to LFSs as the mag-
netic field strengthens, leading to a redistribution of their energy as discussed in
section 4.2.3. The MT cutoff is 80 neV before the linear ramping phase and 115 neV
afterwards. The MT cutoff is linearly interpolated between those values during ramp-
ing. The MT LFS fraction population increases with higher βSS. Spin flips reduce the
effectiveness of the MT cleaning phase, creating more MT LFS than can be cleaned.

4. HFS Cleaning: Cleaning HFSs reduces the likelihood of their spin-flipping into MT
LFSs. The decrease in the MT LFS population during this stage is primarily attributed
to wall reflections, while the absorbers, which move to the middle and bottom posi-
tions, also contribute to the cleaning of some MT LFSs. However, since the duration
of this stage is only 40 s for A and B combined, it does not significantly reduce the
MT fraction.

102



5. Storage: If MT LFSs are lost during this stage, they contribute to a systematic shift
of the measured τst so minimizing this population is crucial for a precise measurement
of τst. For βSS = 2×10−3, there are still more than 10 % marginally trapped neutrons
present at the start of the storage stage. The difference in RMT values between the
runs with different βSS values is seen more clearly in Fig. 4.28 on a log scale. RMT is
lower for lower values of βSS.

6. Ramp-down and Counting: Higher energy neutrons can reach the detectors earlier,
since they can overcome the magnetic barrier earlier during ramp-down. Therefore,
RMT drops inside the storage volume as well as in the cumulative detector counts.

The correlation between βSS and RMT is evident: a lower βSS value decreases the MT
LFS population within the storage volume. Consequently, a lower βSS is expected to reduce
the systematic shift of τst which is influenced by the loss of MT LFSs during the storage
stage.

The MT cleaning stage shows the expected exponential behavior for reducing the MT
LFS population. No significant difference is observed between the three curves for the three
different βSS values during the MT cleaning phase, likely because the spin-flip effect, which
would convert LFSs to HFSs or vice versa, is not as dominant as the absorber-induced loss
effect.

4.3.3 Optimizing the Marginally Trapped Cleaning Time

The neutron lifetime measurement is influenced by systematic effects due to loss processes,
other than β-decay, between 20 s and 1550 s during the storage stage. This has been dis-
cussed in detail in Section 4.2.5. Low-field seekers that are marginally trapped (MT LFSs)
and high-field seekers (HFSs) may be lost through wall interactions during the storage stage.
The magnetically stored LFSs that do not hit the walls are lost only through β−decay or
rest gas interaction. Rest gas interaction is not in the scope of this work and can be found
in [2].

The duration of each cleaning stage affects the number of MT LFSs and HFSs that
survive to the storage stage. This study focuses on optimizing the duration of the MT
cleaning stage to reduce the amount of MT LFSs lost during storage, thereby minimizing
the systematic shift of the measured neutron lifetime ∆τn. In this study, we focus on the
effect of marginally trapped LFSs only. Due to the much smaller number of UCN simulated
compared to a full run at FRM II, high statistical uncertainty was the leading reason to
filter out β−decay from storage stage simulation data for this study. Hence, loss mechanisms
due to MT LFSs have a contribution to the measured storage lifetime of

Minimizing the Systematic Effect Due to Marginally Trapped Neutrons

τMT is the average storage lifetime of all LFS in PENeLOPE during the storage period only
taking into account wall interactions of MT neutrons. Reducing the number of marginally
trapped LFSs in PENeLOPE during the storage stage lowers their impact on the neutron
lifetime measurement by decreasing losses, thereby increasing their storage lifetime τMT.
Consequently, the reduced loss of marginally trapped LFSs decreases this systematic effect,
effectively lowering its contribution to the shift in the measured neutron lifetime, ∆τn.

Each experiment cycle, with different stage times before the storage stage, has its own
τMT. The MT cleaning time is varied in this study, while all other times are taken from Tbl.
4.1. An optimization routine to find the minimum shift ∆τn becomes increasingly difficult as
more stage durations are varied and is out of the scope of this work. This will be investigated
in the future. The range of MT cleaning duration times examined is [0,199] s. During this
stage, the MT LFS population is removed from the storage volume at an exponential rate.
